bullets: JFinBench is a new, refreshable Japanese finance benchmark built from 321 questions in the 2026 editions of six recurring certification exams. It targets accounting, tax, financial planning, and banking, and uses a human-supervised agent pipeline to support construction as new exam editions appear. Why it matters: If you evaluate financial language models, this provides a jurisdiction- and date-specific alternative to static finance tests whose released questions may enter training data. Its refresh model also makes benchmark vintage part of the evaluation decision. Evidence: E001. High confidence.

Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories analyzes 143,209 execution traces from 125 agent configurations and maps raw events into actions such as searching repositories, editing files, and running tests. It reports that agents with similar solve rates can follow substantially different workflows. Why it matters: If you are choosing a coding agent, task success alone may conceal differences in exploration and verification behavior. Trace-level measures can distinguish systems that reach the same score through different operational paths, which affects debugging and deployment review. Evidence: E006. High confidence.

Generated Evaluation Suites as Diversity-Driven Search tests automatically generated agent evaluations by injecting seven controlled defects. For four of five traceable defects, the scenarios covering the defect were too sparse for that defect alone to move the suite’s mean pass rate past the stated detection threshold. Why it matters: If you generate regression suites from specifications, a stable average score does not establish that important defects were tested often enough to register. Suite selection therefore depends on coverage of each failure footprint, not only scenario diversity or mean pass rate. Evidence: E019. High confidence.

Verification Transport introduces matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same agent execution to test whether a language-model verifier keeps its judgment when tool composition, delegation, or history compaction changes which evidence remains visible. Why it matters: If your production agent presents traces differently from your evaluation harness, verifier accuracy measured on full logs may not transfer. This test makes representation stability a separate acceptance criterion for automated judges. Evidence: E022. Medium confidence.

Can You Trust Your Finance Agent? reruns one shipped financial-research agent seven times on 18 questions. Identical runs satisfy between 105 and 123 of 149 rubric criteria, while the reported bill varies by as much as 17%; the study also assigns sampled failures to instruction, tool, model, or data owners. Why it matters: If you are validating an agent for repeatable professional work, one leaderboard run cannot characterize either reliability or cost. Repeated trials plus failure ownership can determine whether a proposed fix belongs in the prompt, tool layer, model, or data. Evidence: E059. Medium confidence.

PerfArena is a new reproducible arena that evaluates generated code across multiple programming languages using execution time, memory, and energy alongside correctness. Why it matters: If you are selecting a code-generation model for frequently executed software, correctness-only benchmarks omit operating costs that can change the product choice. PerfArena supplies a protocol for comparing those resource dimensions directly. Evidence: E058. Medium confidence.
bullets_zh: JFinBench 是一个全新的、可刷新的日本金融基准，基于六项定期举行的认证考试之 2026 年版中的 321 道题构建。它面向会计、税务、财务规划和银行业务，并采用有人类监督的智能体流水线，以便在新版考试发布时支持基准构建。Why it matters: 如果你要评估金融语言模型，它提供了一个针对特定司法管辖区和特定日期的替代方案，可取代那些已发布题目可能进入训练数据的静态金融测试。其刷新模式也使基准版本成为评估决策的一部分。Evidence: E001. High confidence.

Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories 分析了来自 125 种智能体配置的 143,209 条执行轨迹，并将原始事件映射为搜索代码仓库、编辑文件和运行测试等操作。研究报告称，解题率相近的智能体可能采用截然不同的工作流。Why it matters: 如果你正在选择编码智能体，仅看任务成功率可能会掩盖智能体在探索和验证行为上的差异。轨迹级度量可以区分通过不同操作路径取得相同分数的系统，而这会影响调试和部署审查。Evidence: E006. High confidence.

Generated Evaluation Suites as Diversity-Driven Search 通过注入七种受控缺陷，测试自动生成的智能体评估。对于五种可追踪缺陷中的四种，覆盖相应缺陷的场景过于稀少，以至于仅凭该缺陷不足以使评估套件的平均通过率变化超过所述检测阈值。Why it matters: 如果你根据规范生成回归测试套件，稳定的平均分并不能证明重要缺陷得到了足够频繁的测试，足以在结果中显现。因此，测试套件的选择取决于对每种故障影响范围的覆盖，而不能只看场景多样性或平均通过率。Evidence: E019. High confidence.

Verification Transport 为同一次智能体执行引入了相互匹配的原生视图、抽象视图和还原视图，用于测试当工具组合、任务委派或历史压缩改变了仍然可见的证据时，语言模型验证器能否保持其判断。Why it matters: 如果生产环境中的智能体以不同于评估框架的方式呈现轨迹，那么在完整日志上测得的验证器准确率可能无法迁移。该测试将表征稳定性设为自动化裁判的一项独立验收标准。Evidence: E022. Medium confidence.

Can You Trust Your Finance Agent? 针对 18 个问题，将一个已交付的金融研究智能体重复运行七次。相同运行满足 149 项评分标准中的 105 至 123 项，而报告的费用差异最高可达 17%；该研究还将抽样发现的失败归因于指令、工具、模型或数据的负责人。Why it matters: 如果你正在验证一个用于可重复专业工作的智能体，单次排行榜运行既无法刻画可靠性，也无法刻画成本。重复试验与失败归属分析可以确定拟议的修复应落在提示词、工具层、模型还是数据上。Evidence: E059. Medium confidence.
PerfArena 是一个全新的可复现竞技场，在评估多种编程语言生成代码的正确性时，同时考察执行时间、内存和能耗。Why it matters: 如果你正在为频繁执行的软件选择代码生成模型，只考察正确性的基准会忽略可能改变产品选择的运营成本。PerfArena 提供了一套可直接比较这些资源维度的协议。Evidence: E058. Medium confidence.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to finance, creating a need for benchmarks that evaluate their capabilities across financial systems with different regulations and practices. However, existing financial benchmarks provide limited coverage of country-specific financial systems, and they are difficult to keep up to date as released questions leak into training data. We introduce JFinBench, a Japanese financial benchmark comprising 321 examples from the 2026 editions of six regularly administered certification exams covering accounting, tax, financial planning, and banking. To construct it, we develop a human-in-the-loop agentic pipeline in which a coding agent writes exam-specific conversion code and a review page, while a human verifies every example and feeds corrections back to the agent. This pipeline adapts to heterogeneous exam formats and reduces the effort of incorporating new exam editions, enabling periodic refreshes that mitigate data contamination. Evaluating 12 recent LLMs, we find that Claude Fable 5 and GPT-6 Astra exceed 93% overall, while even the best open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, trails Claude Fable 5 by 12 percentage points. When models can additionally use a terminal and web access, they retrieve the knowledge they lack and every model improves. The gap narrows but about 4 points remain, and the ranking of models stays largely the same, suggesting that knowledge held in the model itself remains valuable even with tools. We release the dataset, the evaluation code, and the construction pipeline.
evidence_items.title: JFinBench: A Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams

evidence_items.summary: This repository provides the dataset accompanying the GEMS-GER benchmark for machine-learning-based groundwater modeling. It includes long-term groundwater-level time series, meteorological and hydrological forcing data, site-specific environmental properties, and benchmark results. The data originate from official public sources and have been harmonized across Germany’s 16 federal states (Bundesländer). The benchmark is described in Ohmer et al. (2026), “GEMS-GER: a machine learning benchmark dataset of long-term groundwater levels in Germany with meteorological forcings and site-specific environmental features”. Contents of this repository: Groundwater-level time series (GEMS-GER data/dynamic/MW .csv): Weekly data from 3,207 monitoring wells for 1991–2022, including: Daily temperature (mean, minimum and maximum) Precipitation and humidity (HYRAS/DWD) Actual, potential and reference evapotranspiration Soil moisture and soil temperature at 5 cm depth Snow water equivalent, snowmelt and runoff (ERA5-Land) GWL flag, indicating observed and imputed values Static site descriptors (GEMS-GER data/static/static features.csv): Hydrogeology and soil properties Land use and climate classifications Elevation and derived topographic parameters, such as slope and TWI Benchmark model performance (GEMS-GER data/model performance/): Per-well NSE, RMSE, R² and Bias for the single-well, global dynamic-only and global dynamic-plus-static models. Scores are calculated from the pointwise median predictions of 20 ensemble members per model.
evidence_items.title: GEMS-GER: A Machine Learning Benchmark Dataset of Long-Term Groundwater Levels in Germany with Meteorological Forcings and Site-Specific Environmental Features

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents increasingly review code, yet whether they catch the privacy defects that laws such as the GDPR require software to avoid remains largely untested, partly because few datasets connect real privacy defects to their accepted fixes and review context. We present PrivacyPR, a dataset of 4,131 merged GitHub pull requests (PRs) from 1,469 repositories, created between June 2018 and January 2024. Each PR includes its commits, diffs, review discussion, and LLM-generated labels for privacy relevance, fix type, and GDPR principles. PrivacyPR provides 1,169 high-confidence privacy fixes and 1,643 non-fix PRs, together with Verified, a manually checked split of 250 privacy fixes and 250 non-fix PRs, and Small, a 100 + 100 subset for evaluation. On Verified, both annotators endorsed 72% of the LLM's GDPR-principle assignments. Beyond supporting empirical study of how privacy defects arise and are fixed, PrivacyPR provides a benchmark for privacy-aware code review on real, developer-accepted fixes. Its evaluation harness reverts each fix to reintroduce the defect. On Small, two coding agents detect only 42-51% of defects under a generic review prompt, but 88-91% when explicitly asked to check privacy, while flagging 11-15% of non-fix PRs. These results show that privacy defects can be detected by coding agents, but that detection depends strongly on review intent and comes with false alarms. Data, code, reviews, judge verdicts, and an extensible evaluation harness are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23744765.
evidence_items.title: PrivacyPR: A Dataset of Real-World Privacy Fixes for Benchmarking Privacy-Aware Code Review

evidence_items.summary: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, and audit its predictions against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. We find that agents with similar solve rates can nevertheless differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify code. Moreover, without using task outcomes, token counts, or tool names as features, aggregate behavioral profiles retrieve the corresponding agent stack across disjoint repository sets and programming languages, although task composition is not fully controlled in the cross-repository setting. Through analyses of frontier models and agent scaffolds, we further show that scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift agents' search, editing, and testing behavior. We release the deterministic parser together with the full annotation and analysis pipeline alongside an annotated trajectory subset.
evidence_items.title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories

evidence_items.summary: Agentic time series forecasting extends conventional approaches beyond one-shot numerical prediction toward autonomous, context-aware interaction. However, existing benchmarks offer limited integrated support for diverse contextual information, forecasting-specific adaptive interactions, and systematic evaluation of forecasting agents. In this paper, we introduce CastWorld, an agentic benchmark for context-aware time series forecasting. First, its context-rich dataset suite spans 8 domains and 25 real-world datasets, covering external variables, events, and historical cases under a unified context specification. Second, a lightweight, modular forecasting-native harness provides 49 core tools and a state-adaptive loop that tracks forecast versions and enables iterative evidence gathering and forecast revision. Intermediate forecasts can expose information gaps, while newly acquired evidence guides subsequent revisions and final version selection. Third, model-level evaluation assesses forecast quality, process execution, behavioral trustworthiness, and resource efficiency through decision trajectories and forecast-version histories. Also, systems-level evaluation compares predictive accuracy across forecasting systems. Experiments reveal distinct decision behaviors among agents with comparable accuracy. Additional interactions do not necessarily improve forecasts, and agents may fail to select their best previously generated predictions. Allowing evidence acquisition during forecast refinement improves task-aware forecast scores across all three evaluated models. CastWorld provides a reusable foundation for evaluating agentic time series forecasting under controlled conditions.
evidence_items.title: CastWorld: Benchmarking Context-Aware Agentic Time Series Forecasting Beyond Predictive Accuracy

evidence_items.summary: VEP DATASET STANDARD3 is a curated clinical dataset of transient pattern-reversal visual evoked potentials (VEPs), developed to support reproducible research in clinical neurophysiology, biomedical signal processing, and automated electrophysiological assessment. The openly released component (Part H) contains 119 averaged VEP responses from 38 adult participants, including 88 normal and 31 pathological responses, recorded at Mohammed VI University Hospital of Tangier, Morocco. Recordings were acquired using two clinical stimulation protocols and harmonized to a sampling frequency of 1,000 Hz, with 400 samples per response covering the 0 to 399 ms post-stimulus interval. Each response is accompanied by two sub-averages, enabling estimation of residual noise, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and split-half reliability. The dataset includes pseudonymized participant information, acquisition parameters, response-level clinical labels, documented label provenance, clinician-annotated P100 latencies, and waveform polarity information. Clinical labels distinguish electrophysiologically normal and pathological responses and do not necessarily represent disease diagnoses. The release provides signal recordings in CSV and compressed NumPy (NPZ) formats, structured metadata in TSV files, and predefined subject-grouped cross-validation splits consisting of five repetitions of five folds. These partitions support subject-independent evaluation and reduce the risk of data leakage caused by including responses from the same participant in both training and testing sets. Technical validation includes normative measurements of N75, P100, and N135 components, signal quality assessment, waveform reproducibility, agreement between automatic and clinician-defined P100 latencies, and analysis of age-related effects.
evidence_items.title: VEP_DATASET_STANDARD3: an open clinical dataset of pattern-reversal visual evoked potentials with sub-averages, label provenance and subject-grouped benchmark splits

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Calibration and scope choices determine what set-theoretic estimands represent, yet applied studies often treat them as neutral preprocessing. We benchmark the recovery and false-detection behaviour of Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) using a public-service measurement framework motivated by five rural services in Vietnam. The evaluation uses 456,000 synthetic datasets from 456 scenarios with 1,000 replications each. Scenarios vary sample size, measurement error, condition correlation, cellwise missingness, outcome resolution, missingness mechanism and two data-generating processes: a two-condition gate and a substitutive non-gate. Across the 432-scenario missing-completely-at-random factorial, fsQCA calibrated with substantive 2/3/4 anchors recovered the programmed gate in 0.749 of replications and falsely detected the pair in 0.015 of non-gate replications. Raw-score NCA yielded rates of 0.673 and 0.087, respectively. NCA applied to 2/3/4 fuzzy memberships was conservative (0.049 recovery), whereas percentile-calibrated fsQCA was less specific (0.519 recovery; 0.162 false detection). In matched scenarios, increasing sample size improved semantic-anchor fsQCA recovery but reduced raw NCA recovery as observations filled the ceiling region. These results show that calibration anchors and NCA scope definitions are part of the estimand. Applied studies should preregister external anchors, report scope and algorithmic non-results, and test recovery against a plausible counterfactual data-generating process. The benchmark evaluates analytical workflows; it does not estimate how Vietnamese residents assess public services.
evidence_items.title: Calibration and Configurational Recovery in NCA and fsQCA: A Monte Carlo Benchmark for Public-Service Research in Vietnam

evidence_items.summary: Abstract As conversational AI expands into emotionally sensitive domains such as mental health support and counseling, empathetic response generation has become a key research challenge. Existing empathetic dialogue systems either reflect the user’s surface level emotions or, when relying on external commonsense knowledge bases, capture only generic patterns. We propose a Theory of Mind inspired framework in which a large language model first infers the speaker’s five mental states of Belief, Desire, Emotion, Intent, and Knowledge from the multi turn dialogue history and then uses them as conditioning signals for empathetic response generation. A preliminary study on a theory of mind benchmark indicates that the LLMs employed perform reasonably on mental state inference in both multiple choice and free form settings. On an empathetic dialogue dataset, injecting the self generated inferences improved response quality under both automatic metrics and LLM as judge evaluation. In the LoRA fine-tuned setting, the ToM condition performed comparably to COMET, an external commonsense knowledge baseline, with higher ROUGE-L point estimates for all four backbones and a significant advantage for one. Shuffled and corrupted descriptions consistently degraded response quality, whereas the ToM condition and a context-grounded factual-summary control performed similarly, indicating that contextual grounding is the primary source of the benefit. These findings suggest that speaker grounded mental state reasoning can be an effective strategy for empathetic dialogue systems.
evidence_items.title: Theory of mind inspired mental state reasoning with large language models for empathetic response generation

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Molecular simulation workflows based on the GFN family of semiempirical methods (GFN1‐xTB, GFN2‐xTB, GFN0‐xTB, and GFN‐FF) are benchmarked as geometry engines against the original BP86/def2‐SVP DFT level of theory of the Harvard Clean Energy Project (CEP) database for high‐throughput organic photovoltaic (OPV) molecule screening. Two representative datasets are evaluated: a 73‐molecule subset of the CEP database of extended ‐conjugated systems and a 56‐molecule subset of the QM9 database of small organic molecules, selected via variance‐based Neyman allocation from stratified and clustered chemical spaces. Structural fidelity is assessed through heavy‐atom RMSD, radius of gyration, equilibrium rotational constants, bond lengths, and bond angles, and topological consistency via the VF2 graph isomorphism algorithm. GFN1‐xTB and GFN2‐xTB achieve the highest structural fidelity for both datasets, with mean hRMSD values of 0.765 and 0.771 Å for CEP and bond length MADs of 0.018 and 0.021 Å, respectively. GFN2‐xTB achieves the best angle accuracy (MAD = 0.70°) among all methods. VF2 topological failure rates are minimal for CEP (1.4% for both GFN1/2‐xTB workflows) but substantial for QM9 with GFN0‐xTB (26.8%) and GFN‐FF (16.1%), indicating that self‐consistent‐charge methods (GFN1/2‐xTB) provide substantially higher topological reliability than non‐self‐consistent methods for chemically diverse molecular spaces. Meanwhile, GFN‐FF provides the largest computational speedup (up to ∼177× relative to BP86/def2‐SVP) with an empirical ‐like apparent scaling over the sampled molecular size range. Sensitivity analyses across solvation environments, basis sets (def2‐SVP vs. def2‐TZVP), and DFT levels of theory (BP86/def2‐SVP vs. B3LYP/6‐31G(2df,p) for QM9) confirm that method rankings are preserved in all cases (rank correlation ρ > 0.98), validating the primary benchmark as robust for relative method comparison.

evidence_items.summary: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench.
evidence_items.title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers

evidence_items.summary: Generating an evaluation suite from an agent's specification is diversity-driven search: a generator fills a descriptor space (requirements $\times$ personas $\times$ scenario kinds), and the suite it emits is an archive, then scored like a benchmark by its mean pass rate, which throws away the search's product. We inject 7 controlled defects into a $\tau^2$-bench agent across two domains. Coverage yields a ceiling: if a defect's traced footprint holds $b$ scenarios that pass at baseline, it can itself contribute at most $b/N$ to a suite of $N$. For 4 of 5 traceable defects that ceiling lies at or below the detection threshold $\theta = 0.10$, so no within-footprint effect can move the suite past it; in both domains the tool-removal defect destroys every covered scenario it can (exactly its ceiling) while the suite-level pass rate moves the other way. Defects split into two regimes: trace-aligned ones, where per-cell scoring recovers the tool-removal defect in full and reveals a second as a significant improvement, and trace-orthogonal ones, whose footprint is behavioural: forced escalation is detected in retail at a traced coverage of exactly zero. Diversity along the generator's own axes helps only where it aligns: at fixed suite size a happy-path-only suite detects nothing, while a kind-diverse one detects the orchestration defect in 5 of 20 draws. Evaluation archives should be scored per cell and should publish coverage as a first-class property.
evidence_items.title: Generated Evaluation Suites as Diversity-Driven Search for Real Agent Regressions

evidence_items.summary: LLM-based verifiers are increasingly used to evaluate agent executions, but their reliability is typically measured under a single representation of the trajectory. In deployed agent systems, the same execution may be exposed through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, changing what execution evidence is directly observable to the verifier. It therefore remains unclear whether correct verifier judgments persist across such abstraction boundaries. We introduce Verification Transport, a reliability test that measures judgment stability under abstraction-induced changes in execution observability. We construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, realized trajectory, outcome, ground truth, evaluation criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, we find substantial transport failure, reaching about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation. Verification protocols exhibit distinct failure modes: direct verification more often produces incorrect verdicts, whereas evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain under limited observability. This suggests that lower transport failure rates do not necessarily imply greater reliability. Restoring the corresponding execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, while recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable. These results show that native-view accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.
evidence_items.title: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Automated sleep staging has achieved strong bench- mark accuracy; however, clinical adoption remains limited due to a lack of interpretability. In this work, we fill the research gap by extending the SleepXAI sleep staging framework to systematically compare five different XAI methods. Further, attribution fidelity is evaluated using Spearman rank correlation with AASM-defined EEG frequency bands, serving as clinically grounded reference signals. In this paper, we focus on single- channel Electroencephalogram (EEG), which is more amenable to practical clinical deployment compared to full polysomnography setups. Experiments are conducted on the Sleep-EDF benchmark dataset and the DREAMT dataset. In DREAMT, we stratified subjects based on OSA into four Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) severity groups. We observed that the SleepXAI model achieves strong classification performance on both datasets. Among the evaluated methods, Integrated Gradients (IG) consistently achieves the highest mean attribution fidelity across all five sleep stages on Sleep-EDF and across all AHI groups on DREAMT, outperforming all other evaluated methods under the Spearman rank correlation metric. These findings highlight the importance of attribution method selection as a key factor for ensuring reliable and clinically interpretable automated sleep staging systems.
evidence_items.title: Towards Explainable Sleep Stage Classification using Single-Channel Electroencephalogram

evidence_items.summary: We present NER-D, a cross-domain benchmark for German NER comprising 13 datasets spanning 9 domains, including General/Politics, Wikipedia, Legal, Medical, Historical, Financial, Agriculture and Archaeology. We examine the performance of both proprietary LLMs and state-of-the-art small open-source models using normal prompting and further examine the performance gains achievable via in-context learning and LoRA fine-tuning. Our results show that without any sort of optimization a proprietary model (GPT-5.4 mini) outperforms the smaller open-source models on 6 out of 13 datasets, but LoRA fine-tuning enables the smaller models to substantially outperform the proprietary baseline. We further analyze the influence of the domain and the tagset used in each task on the performance achieved in the different evaluation settings. Our benchmark will be available as a resource for the development of future German NER methods on both general and specialized domains.\footnote{We make our code, data, and models publicly available upon acceptance of this paper.
evidence_items.title: NER-D: A cross-domain benchmark for German NER

evidence_items.summary: Web agents powered by large language and vision-language models are increasingly applied to realistic browser work that spans heterogeneous applications, multimodal content, and stateful workflows. However, existing reproducible web-agent benchmarks cover only a small number of web applications drawn from a few software categories, and restrict modality to text and vision. Live benchmarks broaden site coverage but sacrifice reproducibility, since pages and data drift between runs. Moreover, existing benchmarks do not meaningfully evaluate whether agents can understand and use audio and video content embedded within web tasks. To address these gaps, we introduce WebArena-Pro, a benchmark comprising 300 tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications in six domain categories, spanning distinct interface conventions, workflows, and data models. Across the evaluated agents, the best performance is achieved by both Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 at 62.3%, followed by OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro at 60.7%. The strongest GenericAgent configurations, Gemini 3.1 Pro omni and Gemma4 31B, both achieve 30.3%. Among reproducible, human-curated web agent benchmarks, WebArena-Pro provides the broadest application coverage and the most comprehensive multimodal support to date. The benchmark treats audio and video as core observations alongside text and vision, with dedicated actions for extracting information from each. WebArena-Pro runs each task in isolation and supports reproducible, parallel evaluation. Tasks are authored through a dedicated annotator interface, filtered by LLM-assisted triage, and finally validated by humans before release. Project page: https://webarena-pro.github.io
evidence_items.title: WebArena-Pro: A Heterogeneous, Multimodal, Reproducible Benchmark for Web Agents

evidence_items.summary: End-to-end autonomous driving is predominantly evaluated through ego-vehicle safety and task completion. Its deployment in urban traffic, however, creates sustained interactions among vehicles whose collective effects remain insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Ego2Flow, a closed-loop benchmark for assessing the traffic-system impact of autonomous driving on maps distilled from real-world cities. To construct realistic 3D urban environments for sustained closed-loop traffic simulation, we develop an agent-guided map distillation framework that integrates real-world maps and observations with complementary geographic information. Through an iterative feedback mechanism and a traffic information graph that jointly guide scene generation, the framework preserves lane topology, critical road geometry and decision-relevant visual conditions while simplifying nonessential details and completing unobserved regions. Using our proposed framework, we generate and publicly release six CARLA maps from the Argoverse 2 dataset, covering the corresponding real-world regions and enabling paired comparisons of driving behavior under real and simulated observations. On these maps, Ego2Flow evaluates how autonomous driving policies affect traffic efficiency, safety, stability and energy consumption across diverse road structures. Compared with existing construction methods, our framework achieves the lowest average displacement error between planning outputs from paired real and simulated observations. We further benchmark representative driving policies to characterize their system-level impact on urban traffic. Project Page: https://github.com/Fisher-007/Ego2Flow.
evidence_items.title: Ego2Flow: Benchmarking the Traffic-System Impact of Autonomous Driving on Maps Distilled from Real-World Roads

evidence_items.summary: Complete game generation requires agents to coordinate rules, interactions, states, and presentation over a long development process. A single aggregate score obscures which capabilities are implemented and which requirements remain unmet. We present OCTAVE, a benchmark for complete HTML5 game generation organized around eight Capability Dimensions, with 180 tasks and 1,800 Evaluation Requirements drawn from real player requests, commercial-mechanics reconstruction, and human expert design. It covers PC Web, Mobile Web, 2D, and 3D. Requirements distinguish Completeness, assessing publicly specified core implementation, from Richness, assessing hidden, deeper system relationships. Static source-code judgments provide requirement-level diagnosis across capabilities and task conditions. Evaluation of 11 model-harness combinations yields 33.2% Completeness and 32.5% Richness; 19.9% of generation records are static gate failures or missing artifacts. Excluding same-model self-evaluation, even the best combination remains below 50% on both public and hidden requirements. Richness is not harder than Completeness under every task condition. Systems perform relatively better on Core Rules and Numerical Design, while AI/NPC and Feedback and Game Feel show more prominent gaps. Requirement difficulty offers coarse stratification but is only weakly negatively correlated with pass rates. A limited human cross-check finds that requirements judged satisfied by humans but failed by the automated evaluator are the main direction of disagreement. OCTAVE extends evaluation beyond aggregate scores to diagnosis localized by requirement, capability, and task condition.
evidence_items.title: OCTAVE: A Capability-Resolved Benchmark for End-to-End HTML5 Game Generation

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) systems increasingly combine sensed time series with external text such as expert reports and news, yet how reliably models use text that agrees or conflicts with the sensed history remains unclear. We introduce the first real-world diagnostic benchmark organized by text-history relationship: 1,762 text-window pairs across sensor telemetry (Weather), web-service traffic (Wikipedia), and market data streams (Finance), each labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified by whether the text's direction agrees with the historical trend, opposes it, or is not stated. Across ten pretrained models evaluated zero-shot, we investigate text selection and combination under text-history relationships (RQ1) and error diagnosis and horizon-scaled revision control (RQ2). For RQ1, we compare two types of text on paired Weather windows: one directly forecasts temperature changes, while the other describes related weather conditions, such as winds and fronts. Under Aligned, the first type yields the lowest error for most models. Under Conflicting, it increases most models' error above the no-text baseline; we therefore add only its stated magnitude and timing to the second type. Compared with either type alone, this combination lowers mean absolute scaled error (MASE) for six models and raises directional accuracy (DA) for seven. For RQ2, an error decomposition attributes the error increase to oversized revisions, and a training-free rule that limits them outperforms forecasts both with and without text for the four models with this trade-off, lowering MASE by 4.49%-21.98% and raising DA by 2.99%-9.71%. Our dataset is available at https://github.com/Shelton1202/ACU-Bench.
evidence_items.title: Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified? A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multimodal Time Series Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.
evidence_items.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs

evidence_items.summary: Analysis code and processed dataset for a market-scale empirical benchmark of 310 European-market production battery electric vehicles, using manufacturer specifications certified under the Worldwide Harmonised Light Vehicle Test Procedure (WLTP). CONTENTS The deposit contains the analysis dataset (478 vehicles, of which 310 carry complete certified figures) and four Python scripts that reproduce every table and figure in the accompanying article. Running run all.py regenerates the full set of results in roughly two minutes. WHY THE DATASET CARRIES TWO VARIABLE SETS The upstream specification source publishes both manufacturer-certified type-approval figures and its own modelled estimates of real-world performance. A field-identification audit established that three widely used columns hold the modelled estimates rather than the certified values. The choice is consequential: on the same 310 vehicles, the fleet-level correlation between energy consumption and certified range is -0.31 using certified figures and +0.02 using the modelled estimates, and the multivariate consumption elasticity is -0.886 against -0.393. Both variable sets are retained side by side in certified dataset.csv so this comparison can be reproduced directly. KEY RESULTS REPRODUCED Useable battery capacity is the dominant correlate of certified range, with an almost exactly proportional multivariate elasticity (1.013, 95% CI 0.985 to 1.041). Energy consumption carries a partial elasticity of -0.886. evidence_items.summary: Background Acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery (CSA-AKI) is common yet detected late. Risk stratification at the end of surgery could enable timely renal protection, but most machine learning (ML) models either use postoperative data or lack a transparent, pre-specified evaluation. Methods In a retrospective single-center cohort of 1,352 adult cardiac surgery patients (211 AKI, 15.6%), we predicted AKI from 32 routine preoperative and intraoperative (up to end-of-surgery) variables. We benchmarked 210 combinations (five feature-selection strategies × seven algorithms × six class weights) by repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation (10 repeats) on a fixed development set ( n = 1,081), selected the final model by a pre-specified two-stage rule, and evaluated it once on a fixed test set ( n = 271). A screening-oriented threshold (sensitivity ≥0.80) was pre-specified. We additionally tested the few-shot transformer TabPFN, stability selection, bootstrap optimism correction, and simple ensembling, with SHAP for interpretability. Results The selected random forest (positive-class weighting, isotonic calibration) achieved a test-set AUC of 0.722 (95% CI 0.634–0.799), sensitivity 0.762, and specificity 0.515. No model family was decisively superior; penalized linear models generalized comparably, and none of the small-sample strategies or ensembling improved discrimination. Bootstrap correction reduced the apparent AUC from 0.965 to a corrected 0.724. Homocysteine ranked first in SHAP importance and was among ten independent factors in multivariable logistic regression. Conclusion Routine perioperative variables support a screening-oriented, interpretable prediction of AKI at the end of cardiac surgery, with modest discrimination. The lack of model superiority argues for parsimony, and homocysteine merits prospective study; external validation is required before clinical use.
evidence_items.title: Prediction of acute kidney injury at the end of cardiac surgery using routine perioperative variables: a pre-specified benchmark of 210 machine learning combinations

evidence_items.summary: Outlier detection is often run on a random sample because the full dataset is too large. This repository measures resilience to sampling: whether a detector flags the same records when it is fitted on a simple random sample (without replacement) as when it is fitted on the full dataset. Two label-free measures are used: Dice resilience ρ, the overlap of the two flagged lists of equal size, and rank resilience ρ̃, the Spearman correlation of the two score vectors. The accompanying paper groups 16 of the 18 detectors into four classes by the statistic their scores depend on, and analyses how resilience depends on the sample size and the sampling fraction for each class; the other two detectors, k-means scoring and the one-class SVM, are reported as a separate group. The experiments (E1–E8, with E1b and E2b) use 16 benchmark datasets of up to 286,048 records, 13 further datasets for the convergence experiments, and synthetic data. Main result: at a 10% sampling fraction, detectors built on the k-nearest-neighbour graph (Class IV: LOF, KNN, ABOD, Feature Bagging, ADOD) kept on average 48% of their flagged records. The other three classes kept 76% to 82%. Class IV was the least resilient class on all 16 datasets (Friedman test with datasets as blocks, χ²(3) = 32.5, p = 4.2×10⁻⁷). The repository contains the code, the configuration, the result of every replicate, and the scripts that produce every table, figure and number of the paper; the README gives the setup and the commands. The analysis is in the folder analysis/. To cite all versions, use the DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20829792, which always resolves to the latest version.
evidence_items.title: Outlier Detection Methods Are Not Equally Resilient to Sampling

evidence_items.summary: Amodal video object segmentation is fundamentally limited by the absence of datasets that combine real-world complexity with precise ground-truth annotations. To address this, we present Real Video Amodal Segmentation (Real-VAS), a new large-scale, zero-shot evaluation dataset built from composited real-image video. We introduce a novel data generation pipeline that enables the creation of programmatically consistent amodal ground truth for real-world footage, in which the object mask, occlusion boundary, and composited image are all derived from a single unoccluded source, without relying on human estimation or expensive 3D reconstruction. Our dataset is structured into two challenging scenarios: dynamic Occlusion, created by compositing two clips of moving objects, and a unique Container category featuring complex, physically constrained interactions. These container scenarios--On Surface Containment, Articulated Containment, and Mobile Containment--allow us to generate precise ground truth by simulating an object's motion based on its container's tracked transformation. As a result, Real-VAS provides a diverse and challenging benchmark for evaluating amodal segmentation models on realistic video with the precision of synthetic data. The dataset and generation code are publicly available at https://finlay-hudson.github.io/real_vas
evidence_items.title: Real-VAS: a Real-World Video Amodal Segmentation Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Despite remarkable progress in machine translation, Vision Language Models (VLMs) struggle on historical manuscripts, a domain that stresses core Natural Language Processing (NLP) capabilities: low-resource transliteration, archaic vocabulary, and noisy input signals. We present a systematic framework for evaluating the full image-to-translation pipeline on medieval Latin manuscripts, a setting in which scribal shorthand, ligatures, and parchment degradation expose failure modes that are invisible in clean-text benchmarks. Benchmarking on the CATMuS Latin dataset reveals a specialization gap: domain-specific Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models reduce character error rate by up to 4.3$\times$ compared to general-purpose VLMs, despite operating at orders of magnitude fewer parameters. We introduce the Interpres-Parallel-Corpus (IPC), a novel dataset comprising 1,383 aligned manuscript image lines, transcriptions, and expert translations, to our knowledge the first of its kind for medieval Latin. Our experiments uncover a complexity paradox: the simplest pipeline, a specialized OCR model feeding directly into a VLM, outperforms all multi-component variants. Adding retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or post-OCR correction introduces prompt saturation and error propagation that degrade aggregate translation quality. These findings offer both a new benchmark and practical guidance for deploying translation systems in low-resource historical settings.
evidence_items.title: When Simpler Is Better: Evaluating Translation Pipelines for Medieval Latin Manuscripts

evidence_items.summary: Public transit route planning traditionally depends on structured map infrastructure and complex routing engines, and no existing dataset supports training models to bypass this dependency. We present TransitLM, a large-scale dataset of nearly 13 million transit route planning records from four Chinese cities covering 120,845 stations and 13,666 lines, released as a continual pre-training corpus and benchmark data for three evaluation tasks with complementary metrics. Experiments show that an LLM trained on TransitLM produces structurally valid routes at high accuracy and implicitly grounds arbitrary GPS coordinates to appropriate stations without any explicit mapping. These results demonstrate that transit route planning can be learned entirely from data, enabling end-to-end, map-free route generation directly from origin-destination information. The dataset and benchmark are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/GD-ML/TransitLM, with evaluation code at https://github.com/HotTricker/TransitLM.
evidence_items.title: TransitLM: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Map-Free Transit Route Generation

evidence_items.summary: Overview MLIRBench: A Benchmark and Dataset for Compiler and Hardware-Aware Reasoning is a research benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of large language models (LLMs) to reason about program semantics, transformations, and execution behavior in the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR). The benchmark contains 1,768 original–mutated MLIR program pairs, derived from 40 curated PyTorch seed programs, covering 888 linalg pairs and 880 torch pairs across five mutation difficulty levels (L1–L5). MLIRBench includes evaluations of nine language models, comprising 15,912 model reasoning records and 15,907 judged evaluation records. Dataset Contents The release provides nine complementary dataset views: Core: Original and mutated programs with semantic annotations. Master: Consolidated program, mutation, and validation metadata. Reasoning: Model-generated predictions and semantic explanations. Evaluation: Judged model predictions, verdicts, and scores. Errors: Per-model error-related records. Model Arena: Model comparison and evaluation information. Performance: Program-pair runtime measurements where available. Difficulty: Mutation difficulty and aggregated evaluation information. Mutation Provenance: Transformation requirements and validation provenance. All nine views are available in JSONL and CSV formats, with accompanying schema documentation, licensing information, and SHA-256 checksums. Methodology and Intended Use MLIRBench combines dialect-aware program mutations, compiler verification, execution validation using IREE, LLM-based reasoning, and automated judging. The dataset supports research in compiler-aware AI, semantic equivalence classification, program analysis, code reasoning, model evaluation, and fine-tuning, subject to applicable usage restrictions. Data Integrity and Limitations The release has undergone structural consistency checks covering record counts, program identifiers, model coverage, and dataset integrity.
evidence_items.title: MLIRBench - A Benchmark and Dataset for Compiler and Hardware-Aware Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: The complete computational record behind two studies of the catalytic zinc of the bacterial deacetylase LpxC: a crystallographic survey of its first coordination shell across the 75 deposited LpxC–inhibitor complexes with a resolved catalytic zinc, and a docking benchmark in which every pose is scored three ways — by heavy-atom RMSD, by the number of ligand donor atoms placed on the metal, and by the identity of those atoms. The main archive lpxc makale2 veri TAM.tgz contains the input coordinate files, the prepared receptors and ligands in neutral and anionic form, the docking poses from every run configuration, the grid maps and AD4Zn parameter files, the SLURM job scripts, the analysis scripts, the summary result tables and the recorded computing environment. It is unchanged from version 1. Version 2 adds the entry-level inventory of all 102 candidate Protein Data Bank records with the ground for each of the 27 exclusions, which both manuscripts cite as Supplementary Table S1, together with a self-contained script that rebuilds that inventory from the RCSB search and data APIs. README v2 additions.md describes both files, the four selection criteria, and the precedence under which entries failing more than one criterion are counted. The contact-level coordination dataset in this deposit is the primary source for the reference geometry used in the docking study and can be consulted independently of either manuscript. Version 3 adds the GM-DockZn comparison requested in revision. The file gmdockzn zenodo.tgz contains the scripts that prepare GM-DockZn inputs, run the docking and score its poses under the donor-identity criterion, together with the per-method comparison table (Table S4) and the comparison figure (Figure 4). GM-DockZn itself is not redistributed; it is obtained from the authors (www.qmclab.com).
evidence_items.title: LpxC catalytic-zinc coordination: structures, docking outputs and analysis code for 75 inhibitor complexes

evidence_items.summary: Background Effective patient education is essential in pediatric neurology but challenged by time constraints and variable health literacy. Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential solution, yet their accuracy and safety in this specialized field remain incompletely evaluated. Methods In a prospective, blinded benchmarking study, LLM-generated responses to ten standardized pediatric neurology prompts were evaluated. Responses were assessed for factual accuracy, safety, and perceived usability; the study did not assess real-world clinical decision support or caregiver comprehension. A blinded panel of seven consultant pediatric neurology evaluators assessed the outputs using an expert-developed rubric measuring factual accuracy, safety, clinical appropriateness, and usability. The unit of analysis was the scenario-model pair ( n = 40), with median scores across raters used for primary comparisons. Results Linear mixed-effects models revealed significant performance variation across models (F(3,27) = 8.76, p &lt; 0.001). DeepSeek achieved the highest overall composite score (4.01 ± 0.61) and zero safety flags. ChatGPT scored moderately (3.72 ± 0.75) but accounted for most safety issues (5/8), including a contraindicated medication recommendation. Gemini and Perplexity scored lower (3.45 ± 0.77 and 3.38 ± 0.71). The overall composite difference between DeepSeek and ChatGPT was not statistically significant ( p = 0.087). DeepSeek had the highest System Usability Scale score (74.2/100). Presence of any consensus safety flag drastically reduced the odds of expert approval for caregiver-facing use after clinician review (OR: 0.08, p &lt; 0.001). Conclusions DeepSeek produced no consensus safety flags in this benchmark and had the highest expert-rated usability score, but its overall composite score was not statistically different from ChatGPT.
evidence_items.title: Comparative benchmark of four selected large language models for generating patient education content in pediatric neurology: a prospective study

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly accessible to patients with cancer as sources of immediate information about diet, symptoms, supplements, and treatment-related nutritional concerns. Their conversational fluency may create an illusion of clinical adequacy: a response can be well written, plausible, and apparently personalized while remaining incomplete, poorly contextualized, or clinically unsafe. This problem is particularly relevant in oncology nutrition, where advice about restrictive diets, fasting, supplements, malnutrition, sarcopenia, cachexia, and treatment tolerance may have direct implications for patient safety. Existing approaches to evaluating LLM-generated health information use heterogeneous criteria, including accuracy, completeness, readability, usefulness, personalization, evidence support, trust, safety, and potential harm. Classical instruments such as DISCERN, the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool, and the JAMA benchmarks address selected dimensions of health information quality, whereas contemporary LLM-specific frameworks increasingly account for conversational, clinical, and safety-related features. However, these approaches are not specifically designed for oncology nutrition and do not consistently operationalize a non-compensatory logic in which clinically serious safety concerns are assessed separately from otherwise favorable response qualities. We propose a conceptual and operational framework for evaluating patient-facing LLM-generated oncology nutrition responses. The framework treats scientific, clinical, and nutritional appropriateness; clinical and nutritional safety; communication quality and patient utility; transparency; and system-level robustness as conceptually distinct and non-substitutable evaluation dimensions. It also introduces critical safety flags intended to identify veto-level concerns that should not be averaged with favorable performance in other domains.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating large language model-generated oncology nutrition responses: a conceptual framework and validation roadmap

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language model (LLM)-based chatbots are increasingly used for health information, but their suitability for melanoma public education requires evaluation across accuracy, information quality, transparency, and readability. Methods We compared ChatGPT-5.6, DeepSeek-V4, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.5 Flash. Validity was assessed using 200 melanoma-related single-best-answer multiple-choice questions administered in three independent trials. Fifteen core public-education questions were developed from worldwide Google Trends data and clinical experience. Responses were evaluated using DISCERN, EQIP, GQS, and JAMA benchmarks, and readability was assessed using ARI, Coleman–Liau, FKGL, FRES, GFI, and SMOG indices. Results Mean MCQ accuracy was highest for ChatGPT-5.6 (94.0% ± 0.5%), followed by Gemini 3.5 Flash (92.5% ± 1.3%), Claude Sonnet 5 (87.2% ± 1.4%), and DeepSeek-V4 (79.3% ± 0.3%; p &lt; 0.001). ChatGPT-5.6 achieved the highest DISCERN (52.07 ± 9.48), EQIP (81.67 ± 4.08), and GQS (4.40 ± 0.51) scores. JAMA transparency scores were low across models. Gemini 3.5 Flash showed the most favorable overall readability profile; however, mean grade-level indices for all models exceeded the sixth-grade benchmark, and all mean FRES scores were below the recommended range. Conclusion Current LLM chatbots show substantial potential for melanoma education, but performance varies across validity, quality, transparency, and readability. Their use should remain supplementary, with improved source transparency and health-literacy–appropriate language required before broader patient-facing implementation.
evidence_items.title: Validity, reliability, and readability of large language model chatbots for melanoma public education: a cross-sectional comparative study

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Climate change is increasing temperatures and worsening extreme heat[1–5]. Heat threatens human and natural systems[2,3,5–7]. In cities, urban heat islands and concentrations of people, infrastructure, and economic activity amplify risks[6,8–12]. Cities are adapting to heat, yet evidence remains fragmented and difficult to compare because adaptation is multidimensional, context-specific, and scale-dependent[3,6,7,12–18]. Here we introduce and apply the Heat Adaptation Benchmark, a multi-criteria framework for evaluating heat adaptation through structured expert judgment. Twenty-four expert evaluators assessed a purposive sample of 46 cities spanning six global regions and differing in three city characteristics: metropolitan area population, country-level economic resources, and historical climate. Across all cities, the mean total score suggested considerable scope to strengthen documented heat adaptation (36.1 out of 72). Of the six criteria, risk assessment had the highest mean score (8.4 out of 12) and monitoring and evaluation the lowest (3.4). In every city, the combined score for risk assessment, planning, and actions exceeded that for strategy, monitoring and evaluation, and governance. Higher-scoring cities had different combinations of strengths and gaps and were found in every region and city characteristic category. Our results highlight challenges in translating documented assessment, planning, and identified actions into sustained implementation and demonstrated heat risk reduction. We anticipate that the benchmark will support cross-city comparison and learning by illustrating a range of heat adaptation approaches and identifying practices that cities facing similar conditions or challenges could draw on. Across contexts, our findings point to the importance of durable institutions that can implement heat adaptation plans, sustain action through long-term strategies and reliable funding, and assess whether those actions reduce heat risk.
evidence_items.title: A global benchmark of urban heat adaptation

evidence_items.summary: The increasing demand for clean and sustainable energy has accelerated the adoption of solar photovoltaic (PV) systems across residential, commercial, and industrial sectors. However, solar power generation is highly dependent on environmental conditions, including solar irradiance, ambient temperature, cloud cover, humidity, and wind speed. These variations create challenges in maintaining power system stability, balancing electricity demand and supply, and efficiently managing energy storage. Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers promising solutions to these challenges through advanced forecasting, intelligent decision-making, and automated energy management. This paper presents a comprehensive review of AI-based techniques for solar energy forecasting and management, focusing on machine learning (ML), deep learning, weather data integration, and smart energy systems. Methods such as Random Forest, Support Vector Regression, Artificial Neural Networks, Long Short-Term Memory networks, and hybrid forecasting models are discussed in terms of their operating principles, applications, advantages, and limitations. The paper also examines the integration of AI with smart grids, battery energy storage systems, demand-side management, and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies. Furthermore, forecasting evaluation metrics, implementation challenges, and future research directions are outlined. The review indicates that combining historical generation data with weather forecasts and real-time measurements can support more reliable solar power prediction and improve operational decision-making. The paper concludes that AI can play a significant role in developing efficient, resilient, and sustainable solar energy systems, although practical performance depends on data quality, model selection, and validation under real-world conditions.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence In Solar Energy Forecasting and Management

evidence_items.summary: Synonymous coding DNA sequence (CDS) design for plant expression constructs must balance host codon adaptation against guanine-cytosine (GC) composition, restriction-site avoidance, and sequence-integrity constraints, yet benchmark outcomes can depend strongly on the chosen codon-usage reference. Using FactorForge v3.2.0, an open-source CDS design and sequence-review workflow, we evaluated four rule-based design presets (Balanced, High-CAI, GC-target, and Assembly-friendly) on 49,257 reference-derived Nicotiana benthamiana CDS/protein records from the Sol Genomics Network (SGN) QLD183 resource (seed 320), scoring sequence integrity, a historical 55-65% GC window, and absence of BsaI/BpiI/BsmBI sites. With the legacy packaged codon reference, Assembly-friendly passed all three criteria for 63.37% of records (single fixed per-record seed 320; subject to multi-percentage-point variation across independent seed streams); with three genome-derived references its combined pass rate was 0.00% after rounding, whereas GC-target attained 22.68% in each derived condition. A separate v3.3.0 dynamic-programming (DP) execution maximizing the codon adaptation index (CAI) within the same GC window found a GC-compliant sequence for 99.83% of records (49,173/49,257; 84 NO FEASIBLE CDS; mean feasible CAI 0.9989), but 28.21% passed all criteria because Type IIS sites are outside the 1DP objective. An independent FactorForge v3.6.4 2x2 factorial evaluation (N = 49,257) crossing codon reference (legacy C1 vs. high-confidence NbeV1.1 C4) and target GC window (55-65% vs.
evidence_items.title: Constraint-Aware Coding-Sequence Design for Nicotiana benthamiana: A 49,257-Record Benchmark and Codon-Reference Sensitivity Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Reduced-order models of the Kilowatt Reactor Using Stirling TechnologY (KRUSTY ) heat-pipe microreactor test are usually scored against curves digitized from published figures. This paper asks which of their apparent gains survive when the heat-load forcing is not measured independently. We reconstruct source-tagged power and outer-fuel-temperature series and grade the evidence at three levels: calibration (8–12 h), transfer to a later window (20–28 h), and a forward prediction (16–19.8 h) driven only by the documented reflector-platen movements. All five 20–28 h heat-load amplitudes are back-inferred from the power record of the same test, so the transfer is a transfer of thermal parameters, not an independent-input validation. Under a common load input, two thermal stores reduce the 20–28 h power root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 63.9–65.7% relative to one store. Normalized by the mean power of that window, the error falls from 15.4% to 5.6%; in absolute terms it falls from 0.278 to 0.101 kW, and the temperature RMSE from 3.60 to 1.89 °C. A third store lowers the power RMSE only to 0.096 kW, while one of its conductances reaches its upper bound, and with the fuel capacity varied the fitted total storage stays near 19.3 kJ/K, so the data constrain the total storage rather than its distribution. Among the model orders tested, two stores therefore give the best-supported balance between residual reduction and parameter stability. In an out-of-window forward evaluation that uses no post-event output and an observed initial state, the two-store model reaches 0.376 kW and 4.99 °C. The contribution is therefore a reproducible benchmark and an evidence-grading procedure, not a claim of accuracy superior to high-fidelity models.
evidence_items.title: When Does a Two-Node Thermal Model Suffice? An Evidence-Graded Reduced-Order Benchmark for the KRUSTY Heat-Pipe Microreactor Test

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Access to high-quality, FAIR health data is essential for advancing epidemiological, public health and clinical research. NFDI4Health, one of the consortia of Germany’s National Research Data Infrastructure (NFDI), was established in 2020 to address this need by improving data FAIRness for the scientific community. During the initial funding phase, NFDI4Health developed key infrastructure components and services focusing on interoperability, data sharing and research support. Our approach was guided by user needs and real-world use cases in alignment with (inter)national FAIR standards and infrastructures. We advanced findability of health data by establishing a central Health Study Hub and connecting it to local infrastructures, e.g., through the Local Data Hub software, to facilitate transfer of metadata from the local infrastructures to the Health Study Hub. Accessibility was improved by expanding the German Research Data Portal for Health (FDPG) to provide central access to study data and by providing tools to support anonymisation and synthetic data generation. We also developed an interoperable metadata schema for publishing study data and implemented it in the Health Study Hub. To further improve interoperability, a NFDI4Health FAIR sharing collection and AI support for metadata annotation and harmonisation workflows were established. To enhance reusability, data quality assessment tools were further developed, and two frameworks for federated analysis of sensitive health data were piloted. Intensive engagement with our communities through training, advisory services, and collaborative development ensured user relevance. NFDI4Health has established a scalable, interoperable, and user-centred infrastructure to support FAIR data sharing in health research.
evidence_items.title: Advancing FAIR sharing for epidemiological, clinical and public health study data: the German National Research Data Infrastructure (NFDI4Health)

evidence_items.summary: Researchers increasingly rely on people to produce data through online interfaces. Agentic browsers create a new challenge for these workflows because they can navigate websites and complete tasks on a user’s behalf with little technical knowledge or effort. We evaluate whether three consumer-facing agentic browsers can complete online surveys and whether recently proposed measures can detect or prevent their use. The agents received only one simple instruction, "Fill out this survey", without detailed prompting or technical optimization. We tested technical screening measures, visible and invisible CAPTCHAs, AI-specific prompt-injection checks, consistency across a longer survey, and the completion of several surveys from a single instruction. The agents completed surveys with little or no user input, maintained assigned demographic profiles, and passed all tested prompt-leaking and jailbreak-style checks. Browser metadata did not reveal automated participation, and invisible reCAPTCHA was consistently passed by some browsers. Visible reCAPTCHA created the strongest barrier, although agents could sometimes solve it or return control to the user. These findings show that widely available AI agents can take over tasks intended for human participants while producing responses that appear coherent and plausible. This raises broader questions about how researchers can verify that supposedly human-generated data were actually produced by humans.
evidence_items.title: "Fill Out this Survey": Capabilities and Detection of Agentic Browsers

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents BodySync AI, a multimodal calorie-tracking prototype that combines optical character recognition (OCR), object detection, pose estimation, and an agentic large language model (LLM). The system supports two tasks: extracting nutritional values from photographs of food-packaging labels, and analyzing body proportions from full-body images. Nutrition extraction uses a classical image-processing front end (perspective correction, denoising, illumination normalization, and contrast enhancement) followed by EasyOCR and rulebased parsing of calories, fat, carbohydrates, and protein. In parallel, we train a YOLOv8n nutrition-label detector on the Open Food Facts Nutrition Table Detection dataset and study the effect of training epochs, learning rate, optimizer, batch size, and input resolution in 14 controlled runs. The best configuration reaches an mAP@50 of 0.904 and an mAP@50-95 of 0.727 on the validation split. Body analysis uses MediaPipe Pose landmarks to compute normalized shoulder width, hip width, torso length, and shoulder-to-hip ratio, which feed a baseline rule-based bodytype estimate. A Groq-hosted Llama 3.1 8B agent exposes these components as tools through a natural-language interface. We describe the system as built, report the detector experiments, and outline the evaluations and learned body-composition models planned as future work.
evidence_items.title: BodySync AI: A Multimodal Agentic System for Nutrition Label Extraction and Pose-Based Body Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Industry now relies on LLMs to write a large share of production code. Although that code is mostly, but not always, correct, correctness alone does not determine whether it is fit for repeated and extensive use, which depends on what the code costs in time, memory and energy. Most code-generation benchmarks nonetheless evaluate correctness in isolation, and most performance-oriented benchmarks cover few languages and rarely measure energy consumption. To address this gap, we present PERFARENA, an open-source, reproducible arena that ranks LLMs by the performance of their generated code across multiple languages and competitions. PERFARENA executes the solutions of each LLM on a Unix-like host and reports correctness together with latency, peak memory, and energy consumption. Correctness oracles, performance oracles, profilers, and code-generation workflows are pluggable in PERFARENA, enabling the integration of new judging backends and measurement tools without changing the pipeline. We evaluate PERFARENA on two competitions: CLBGComp, 10 compute-intensive benchmarks from the Computer Language Benchmarks Game, and LeetCodeComp, 99 LeetCode problems whose accepted solutions differ measurably in latency. Currently, PERFARENA holds 9,455 correct and measured solutions from 13 state-of-the-art LLMs across 7 programming languages. Across both competitions, got-6-astra is the only LLM that no other LLM beats significantly in latency, energy consumption, or peak memory, solving 99.7% of LeetCodeComp and 100% of CLBGComp. All PERFARENA leaderboards and measured solutions are publicly available, providing a continuously updated reference that helps developers choose an LLM per language and metric, instead of relying only on correctness rates or pricing.
evidence_items.title: PerfArena: Ranking LLMs by Code Performance

evidence_items.summary: Can you trust a finance agent you did not build? We take the reference agent shipped with the Vals Finance Agent Benchmark v2, leave it untuned, and ask four questions a leaderboard score does not answer. Is the score stable? Seven identical runs on 18 questions pass between 105 and 123 of 149 rubric criteria, and the bill varies by up to 17%. When the agent fails, who owns the fix? We classify 20 failed trajectories, from three runs of nine held-out questions, by the layer whose owner would remedy them, under a taxonomy frozen in advance: 13 belong to the agent's instructions, 3 to its tools, 4 to the model, none to its data. Can that diagnosis be trusted? Four blind readers from three model families, given only the traces, name the same fault as our LLM analyzer in 94% of cases, the rate at which they agree with one another (93%). Can a change be trusted? An optimization loop reads the traces, makes one targeted change per round and keeps it only if it clears a fixed threshold. Under a cost objective its final configuration costs 0.34x the baseline on the held-out questions (95% CI [0.22, 0.58]) at accuracy within noise. Under an accuracy objective it gains 14 points on the development questions and 1.5 on the held-out ones (CI [-5.3, +7.2]). Judged against the measured run-to-run noise, under a rule written before the test was opened, the first is a real saving and the second is not. This is a case study of one agent and nine test questions, not a general result.
evidence_items.title: Can You Trust Your Finance Agent? Drift, Diagnosis and Auditable Intervention on One Shipped Financial Research Agent

evidence_items.summary: We introduce GDP_xlsx, a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with an expert rubric of binary criteria and with the complete workbook or CSV file it refers to. Together the files hold 2.18 million populated cells, and the rubrics 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, and an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric. Completeness and exclusivity criteria require set-valued answers to be found in full and with nothing extra. We rank models by strict pass@1, the share of attempts that meet every criterion. Across 20 model configurations, including frontier models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the top-scoring one, Gemini 4 Argon, passes only 38.3% of attempts, and the median score is 19.3%, leaving wide headroom. We release the evaluation harness and three public tasks; the other 67 are held out to protect the leaderboard from contamination.
evidence_items.title: GDP.xlsx: Benchmarking Frontier Models on Professional Workbooks

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains static and controlled-motion recordings from a laboratory single-axis open-loop interferometric fiber-optic gyroscope with a 500 m fiber coil, accompanied by ambient temperature measurements from three nearby DS18B20 sensors. Seven HDF5 recordings cover approximately 145.8 hours: two stationary recordings of 58 and 55 hours, three bidirectional constant-rate acquisitions with commanded angular rates from 0.5 to 60 degrees per second, a 14.7-hour slow sinusoidal rotation recording, and a 16-hour recording acquired with phase modulation disabled while the optical source and detector remained powered. Each recording contains the in-phase and quadrature demodulator outputs in volts, ambient temperature measurements on their own time axis, acquisition metadata, and timestamp-integrity information. The nominal gyroscope sampling rate is 1674.107142857 samples per second. No scale-factor conversion is applied to the stored voltage channels. The package also includes commanded-motion schedules, the positions reported by the rate-table controller and the run logs of the three constant-rate acquisitions, Allan deviation curves and noise coefficients, plateau statistics, calibration fits, sinusoidal-block results, figures, a machine-readable inventory, and Python and MATLAB code. The analysis code generates the derived products from the deposited recordings. Four further short rate-table recordings, in the same format and with their logs and fits, are provided in checks/ for the estimates of the scale factor outside the two calibrations. The original instrument MAT chunks and temperature CSV logs are not included; the extraction code is provided to document the conversion procedure. The data support noise characterization, calibration studies, examination of associations with ambient temperature, and the use of measured disturbance sequences in simulation and algorithm evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Static and dynamic recordings from an interferometric fiber-optic gyroscope with laboratory temperature data
