evidence_items.summary: Formulating an optimization problem strongly affects final solution quality, yet good formulations usually require substantial expertise. Recent studies have explored automatically deriving optimization problems from natural-language descriptions, but existing benchmarks focus on settings where objectives and constraints can be written explicitly as mathematical expressions. Many practically important problems are naturally treated as black-box optimization (BBO) problems, in which only objective values are observable, and the functional form is unavailable. In BBO, search space design (as part of problem formulation) and optimization algorithm selection are crucial for problem-solving. Automating these processes with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. We introduce Black-Box Optimization Word Problems (BBOWP), a novel problem setting in which a system must infer both a search space and an optimization algorithm from a natural-language description of a black-box optimization task. To support research on this setting, we establish the BBOWP Benchmark Suite (BBOWP-Bench), a dataset and evaluation framework for BBOWP. Each instance combines a natural-language problem description, an executable evaluation environment, and a human-designed reference formulation, allowing evaluation of both search-space design and algorithm selection. Using this benchmark, we evaluate LLMs on the joint formulation of search spaces and optimizers from natural-language descriptions across multiple BBO domains. We show that current LLMs vary their optimizer choice with the evaluation budget, though they sometimes struggle with search space design, particularly in identifying important variables and balancing their ranges when the problem description is less informative or the search space is highly problem-specific. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/shiralab/bbowp-bench.
evidence_items.title: BBOWP-Bench: Evaluating LLMs on Black-Box Optimization Word Problems

evidence_items.summary: Large language model agents are increasingly expected to negotiate and transact autonomously, yet existing benchmarks rarely combine multimodal product grounding, multi-issue bargaining, and competitive multi-agent markets. We introduce AgenticPay, a unified benchmark for evaluating multimodal agents' ability to reach high-welfare, multidimensional agreements in realistic markets. AgenticPay includes 160 multimodal tasks across four business scenarios (E-commerce, Food Delivery, Ride-hailing, and Apartment Rental) and eight market topologies, from bilateral bargaining to many-to-many competition. Agents interpret product images, infer opponents' hidden preferences, and negotiate binding contract terms such as price, lease duration, return policy, and delivery speed through multi-round natural-language dialogue. A utility-based framework evaluates agreement quality and joint welfare. Experiments with proprietary (GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview) and open-weight (Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, InternVL3-38B) multimodal models reveal substantial limitations in value creation and market reasoning. Even the strongest model, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, achieves a GlobalScore of only 42.3/100. As markets shift from bilateral to multi-sided, average GlobalScore falls by 5.7 points, with open-weight models declining by up to 11.5 points. AgenticPay provides a testbed for evaluating multimodal agents in realistic commerce. Code and data: https://github.com/SAIL-Research-Lab/AgenticPay.
evidence_items.title: From Chats to Markets: AgenticPay for LLM-Powered Negotiation in Multi-Agent Commerce

evidence_items.summary: API misuse in code generated by large language models (LLMs) presents a serious and growing challenge in software development, as although LLMs demonstrate impressive code generation capabilities, their interactions with complex library APIs are often error-prone and can lead to software failures and vulnerabilities. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale study of API misuse patterns in LLM-generated code by analyzing both method selection and parameter usage across Python and Java, using three representative LLMs: StarCoder-7B, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, and GitHub Copilot. Based on extensive manual annotation of 3,209 method-level and 3,492 parameter-level misuses, we identify and categorize four recurring misuse types by building on and refining prior API misuse taxonomies. Our evaluation of the three LLMs reveals persistent challenges in API usage, particularly hallucination and intent misalignment. To address these issues, we propose Dr.Fix, an LLM-based automatic repair approach guided by our taxonomy, which improves repair accuracy compared to baseline prompting and existing repair methods, achieving gains of up to 38.4 BLEU and up to 72 more exact matches on benchmark datasets. This work offers important insights into the current limitations of LLMs in API usage and points to directions for improving automated misuse repair in code generation systems.
evidence_items.title: Identifying and Mitigating API Misuse in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Reproducibility archive for manuscript FPE-D-26-00588, “Grid-based Gibbs-energy initialization of near-critical three-phase CO2–hydrocarbon flash calculations”. Version v1.8.1 includes the original benchmark and supplementary investigations S1–S34. At a regular ternary three-phase boundary, a derivative coefficient links the quadratic Gibbs-energy gap to the linear continued local TPD signal. Frozen predictions of the local threshold-crossing scale are tested using 60- and 80-digit calculations on nine paths at three selected equilibria. Controlled grid and sequential flash experiments distinguish local signal detectability, algorithmic phase retention and phase-amount accuracy. The S34 precision follow-up retains 107 finite-criterion passes in 108 method-state runs, including 60 three-phase results. A separately frozen bounded-feedback extension is evaluated on 54 further new amounts (108 full runs): 108 pass the finite criteria, with 61 three-phase and 47 two-phase results. Feedback activates in one new grid case and recovers it. Earlier failures and outcomes are retained. These finite checks do not certify global stability or universal phase recovery. The archive contains source code, fixed protocols, input and source hashes, stored numerical outputs, traces and verification scripts. The baseline timing comparison does not include the later high-precision and feedback extensions. Version v1.8.1 is an editorial clarification of v1.8.0 and adds no numerical experiments. S1–S31 were previously deposited in v1.4.0 (10.5281/zenodo.24100658); this archive additionally supplies S32–S34. The theoretical expansion is conditional on the regularity assumptions stated in S32. The selected equilibria test the prediction; they do not establish empirical transfer to industrial mixtures or unrelated implementations. MIT applies to original software only. Third-party data terms and source attribution are documented in THIRD PARTY DATA.md.
evidence_items.title: Code and data for: Grid-based Gibbs-energy initialization of near-critical three-phase CO2-hydrocarbon flash calculations

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence has progressed from task-specific systems toward general models spanning perception, generation, reasoning, and autonomous interaction, making reliable evaluation essential for comparison, deployment, and post-training feedback. At scale, modern evaluation pipelines increasingly rely on LLM-as-a-Judge to produce scores, preferences, and critiques; in its fixed-context setting, the judge relies on the supplied evaluand and evaluation materials. Yet a reliable verdict may require evidence beyond the supplied evaluand and context---either because critical environmental states remain unrecorded in the static execution log, or because controversial factual claims require external verification. Passive judges cannot obtain that missing evidence before deciding, especially when evaluating agent trajectories, executable artifacts, or domain-specific reports. Recent work therefore develops active evaluators that seek missing evidence and update their grounds for judgment before deciding. We bring these advances together through Agent-as-a-Judge, focusing on how evaluators construct and control checking processes within the broader LLM-based judging landscape. We define the scope through evaluation-directed checks and the use of their results, covering both structured workflows and observation-driven control. We organize the design space by multi-agent collaboration, tool integration, memory, and planning, and show how these mechanisms supply the checks and evidence on which a verdict rests. We consolidate published scores and reproduce missing entries for key agentic judges; the comparison reveals uneven agentic gains and motivates dedicated agentic evaluation. We conclude by characterizing application demands and open challenges in cost, reliability, safety, and governance that condition trusted deployment of agentic judges at scale.
evidence_items.title: Agent-as-a-Judge

evidence_items.summary: Hallucination benchmarks for text-to-image generation are predominantly designed around diffusion models, limiting their diagnostic value for visual autoregressive (VAR) models and the development of mitigation methods. We identify two limitations in existing prompt construction paradigms: many prompts are no longer challenging for modern generators, while category-based construction relies on recurring object-attribute-relation templates and rarely tests interactions among multiple visual requirements within a single image. We introduce InfiHall-Bench, a controlled benchmark of 411 prompts constructed by systematically composing five foundational and visually verifiable skills: attribute binding, spatial relation, action relation, part consistency, and scene consistency. Each prompt covers 4.05 annotated skills on average, enabling the evaluation of hallucinations under diverse combinations of visual requirements. Using this benchmark, we find that hallucinations in VAR models exhibit a scale-wise persistence pattern: semantic errors can emerge at different autoregressive scales and are rarely corrected by subsequent fine-scale steps. Motivated by this observation, we propose Confidence-Masked Hallucination Mitigation (CMHM), which estimates the prediction confidence of target visual tokens at each autoregressive scale during teacher-forced fine-tuning. CMHM downweights reliably predicted tokens, allowing optimization to focus on uncertain predictions across scales. Experiments show that InfiHall-Bench distinguishes models that existing compositional benchmarks rate as comparable, while CMHM consistently outperforms uniform LoRA fine-tuning for VAR-based text-to-image generation.
evidence_items.title: InfiHall-Bench: A Benchmark for Hallucination Evaluation in Autoregressive Text-to-Image Generation

evidence_items.summary: Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (CGEC) is typically formulated as a text-to-text problem. While suitable for digital texts, this formulation falls short in real-world K-12 education, where AI-assisted corrections are expected directly on essay images, which are primarily handwritten and exhibit many irregularities. To bridge this gap, we introduce Grounded Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (G-CGEC), an image-to-grounded-edit task requiring systems to predict both corrections and their positions on essay images. We propose G-CGEC-Eval, a benchmark comprising real-world images of K-12 Chinese essays with fine-grained annotations. For evaluation, we adapt IoU-based metrics from object detection and propose a more tolerant alternative based on center-distance matching. Using this benchmark, we evaluate open-source and proprietary vision-language models under a direct single-pass setting, as well as settings with auxiliary components (OCR and character grounding) coordinated via pipelining or agentic harnessing. Results show that even top-tier proprietary models perform surprisingly poorly in the single-pass setting, while pipelining and agentic harnessing yield meaningful improvements. Notably, an error-type-based multi-agent workflow achieves the best performance, establishing it as the strongest baseline for future G-CGEC research. Through ablations and fine-grained analysis, we find the task remains far from solved, with linguistic error discovery and character-level grounding as the primary bottlenecks. This underscores the need for models that better integrate visual perception with linguistic reasoning and visual grounding.
evidence_items.title: From Images to Grounded Edits: A Real-World Benchmark for Chinese Grammatical Error Correction in Handwritten Essays

evidence_items.summary: Early detection of genetic kidney diseases, especially autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), is crucial because certain genotypes such as truncating PKD1 mutations cause rapid kidney growth and early progression to end-stage kidney disease. MRI-based genotype inference is a potential low-cost complement to genetic testing. However, although many deep learning methods have been developed for classifying various MR images, applying them to ADPKD remains challenging: (1) abdominal MR images are generally too large to be handled by deep learning models designed for smaller images like brain MRI, and (2) the amount of labeled data for ADPKD genetic mutations is insufficient to train deep learning models. In order to address these challenges, we propose E3PN, an efficient 3D MRI-based ADPKD genotype classification network that relies on point sampling and E(3)-invariance. We utilize a point representation of 3D MRI, which consumes less GPU memory than a voxel representation. For further memory efficiency, 3D points are sampled from a mixture distribution over the two kidneys in each image. Since E(3)-invariance has been shown to improve data efficiency, we also incorporate it into our model through coordinate canonicalization. On our ADPKD dataset, E3PN trains 163 times faster and uses 103x less GPU memory than a 3D ResNet, while also improving F1 from 0.165 to 0.226 over both baselines. These results establish a first benchmark for five-way ADPKD genotype classification from 3D MRI and show that point sampling and coordinate canonicalization yield two-orders-of-magnitude efficiency gains with a modest but consistent improvement in F1.
evidence_items.title: Efficient Genotype Classification from 3D MRI in ADPKD via Density-Aware Point Sampling and E(3)-invariance

evidence_items.summary: Causal discovery promises to find which recorded variables drive a process target such as product quality, yield or energy use. Process data with known causes are rare, and in existing benchmarks the difficulty of identifying the causes of a target is either fixed by the recorded data or set for the whole graph. We present a synthetic benchmark for target-centric causal discovery in industrial processes. Its generator is a two-level structural causal model inspired by batch production, assembled from components that each model one phenomenon of process data, such as a control loop or a delayed effect. The graph is built around the target: without sensor error, every non-cause can be distinguished from the direct causes by conditioning on them or by time order. Each component is set independently, so the difficulty can be varied one condition at a time. We evaluate eight methods, from association measures to effect estimation, with an error analysis by the role of the selected candidate; all degrade as the difficulties combine, each in a way consistent with its assumptions.
evidence_items.title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Target-Centric Causal Discovery in Industrial Processes

evidence_items.summary: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with Federated Learning (FL) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) often complicates optimization. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen $\mathbf{A}$ matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling $\mathbf{A}$ matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50\%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. Furthermore, we show that in this frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ regime, the adaptation rank $r$ directly governs the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the perturbed gradients. Specifically, we find that the SNR increases linearly with $r$, implying that clients' learning rates must be dynamically scaled with their adaptation ranks for higher utility. Building on these foundations, we introduce SPRA-LoRA (Stochastic Projection Rank-Aware LoRA), a federated rank-aware fine-tuning strategy that utilizes frozen, resampled $\mathbf{A}$ matrices and rank-dependent learning rates for clients. We also prove its convergence with heterogeneous client resources. Our experiments across benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPRA-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with half the overhead on clients.
evidence_items.title: Stochastic Projections and Rank-Aware Learning Rates for Federated LoRA

evidence_items.summary: Synthesis planning aiming to find pathways of reactions for a target molecule is one of the most important and challenging tasks in drug discovery. Recent progress has produced both specialized deep-learning retrosynthesis systems and general-purpose large language models, but objective comparison remains difficult due to the lack of flexible, chemically interpretable benchmarking protocols. In the current study, we are introducing the URSA (Utilitarian RetroSynthesis Assessment) evaluation framework that provides the opportunity to benchmark the synthetic routes not only from a formal perspective, such as convergence to commercially available starting materials, but also from a chemical plausibility perspective, mimicking the way expert chemists evaluate the reactions and routes. The study covers a comprehensive evaluation of both conventional end-to-end retrosynthesis solutions and LLMs for the synthesis planning task on a set of novel, diverse target molecules with undisclosed synthetic routes, which represent realistic tasks in the daily drug design routine. Although LLMs can support high-level strategic planning and even achieve SOTA performance in the OOD set, the Pareto frontier for estimated run cost and chemically plausible route solvability consists entirely of specialized retrosynthesis planners.
evidence_items.title: URSA: Chemistry-Aware Benchmark for Utilitarian Retrosynthesis Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist in experimental design, yet fluent protocols often remain physically infeasible. We introduce PhysDox, a physical feasibility auditing benchmark for biomedical protocols comprising a 683-sample expert-curated Gold set and a 5,000-sample Silver set across six sensing domains. We formulate the task as a two-stage evaluation: severity detection classifying protocols as valid, minor, or fatal, followed by the constraint-level diagnosis of fatal violations. Evaluating 6 LLMs across 4 inference strategies yields a peak Stage-1 macro-F1 of only 53.0. Moreover, strong oracle diagnosis collapses during end-to-end evaluation due to correlated cascade errors. Error analysis reveals scaffold bias, where models conflate procedural completeness with physical validity. Consequently, implicit constraints exhibit a 2 times higher miss rate than explicit hardware violations, supported by strong statistical correlation at $\rho{=}0.81$ and $p{<}0.01$. Trace analysis of false negatives exposes a 54%--46% split between attention and judgment failures, ultimately demonstrating that protocol auditing demands calibrated feasibility reasoning rather than factual recall or longer rationales.
evidence_items.title: PhysDox: Benchmarking LLMs on Physical Feasibility Auditing of Physiological Sensing Protocols

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by clinicians, researchers, and trainees to retrieve peer-reviewed references in support of clinical claims. LLMs frequently fabricate citations or attach plausible-sounding but unsupportive references — a failure mode with direct patient-safety and research-integrity consequences. No existing benchmark resource provides a temporally-stratified, diabetes-specific, openly-licensed test set for systematic and reproducible evaluation of LLM citation fidelity. This study introduces DiabCite-700, a temporally-stratified benchmark of 700 citation-anchored clinical claims drawn from 35 landmark peer-reviewed diabetes publications across three publication eras (Stratum A 2026, Stratum B 2025, Stratum C 2020-2024), paired with authoritative gold-standard reference metadata. The locked construction methodology, six-outcome verification taxonomy, composite scoring framework (Strict Score range -7 to +35; Lenient Score 0 to 7; Composite True Support Rate), and demonstration evaluation of twelve contemporary LLM configurations spanning four ecosystems times three reasoning tiers are pre-specified in this preregistration. Six pre-specified outcome families are tested with Holm-Bonferroni family-wise error control: Hard Fabrication Rate, Bibliographic Fidelity, Illusion of Support Rate, Composite True Support Rate, Stability Rate, Confidence Calibration. Six pre-specified sensitivity analyses follow. No human subjects, no patient data, no biological specimens. All source material derives from previously published peer-reviewed literature. Ethics exemption requested from UAEU SSREC and CMHS-REC before data collection begins.
evidence_items.title: DiabCite-700: A Temporally-Stratified Benchmark of Citation Fidelity Across Fast, Pro, and Thinking Tiers of Four Large Language Model Ecosystems in Diabetes Literature

evidence_items.summary: Data, code and simulation outputs supporting the article on graph-based urban heat archetypes in two Mediterranean historic cores: downtown Amman, Jordan, and the Casco Antiguo of Seville, Spain. Building and street archetypes are derived from spatial form alone using a graph convolutional autoencoder, with every thermal and energy variable withheld from training. The fixed partitions are then scored against four independent held-out outcomes: daytime and night-time land surface temperature, simulated pedestrian radiant exposure (mean radiant temperature and UTCI from SOLWEIG), and rooftop photovoltaic yield. Contents. Building and street attribute tables for both cities with archetype assignments; SOLWEIG diurnal simulation output under own and harmonised meteorological forcing, including a canopy-removed Seville counterfactual; rooftop photovoltaic yield and heritage-constrained scenarios; a footprint-typology benchmark; and the revision analyses - a four-classifier comparison, bootstrap and input-perturbation uncertainty, and a check of the modelled shadow geometry against satellite land surface temperature. Verification. Run python docs/verify results.py from the deposit root. It reproduces the published partition sizes exactly and the published effect sizes to within 0.001, and confirms the documented convention for the modelled sun-exposure field. OpenStreetMap. Building footprints and street centrelines derive from OpenStreetMap, which is licensed ODbL 1.0. No OpenStreetMap geometry or tags are redistributed here, so that this deposit can be released under CC BY 4.0. Each feature retains its osm id and a centroid (centroid lon, centroid lat, EPSG:4326); code/rebuild geometry.py re-fetches full geometry from OpenStreetMap. Anything that recombines this deposit with OpenStreetMap geometry is a Derivative Database and must be released under ODbL 1.0 with attribution to OpenStreetMap contributors. Scope. This deposit reproduces the published tables and figures.
evidence_items.title: Relational Graph Learning for Urban Heat Archetyping and Cross-City Transfer

evidence_items.summary: The reliability of quadcopters is becoming increasingly important. However, the field of quadcopter fault diagnosis lacks a standardized, reproducible benchmark for fair and comprehensive algorithm evaluation. To address this gap, this paper presents RflyBench-FD, a standardized, open benchmark for quadcopter fault diagnosis built upon the RflyMAD dataset, publicly accessible at https://www.rflybench.com/competitions/5/. RflyBench-FD establishes a complete evaluation framework that covers eight representative fault types and provides standardized simulation/real dual-domain splits, a well-defined task formulated as eight parallel classification sub-tasks, publicly released scoring scripts, and a multi-dimensional metric system (accuracy, F1-score, and robustness under Gaussian noise at 8/4/2[Formula: see text]dB SNR and physically motivated sensor degradations) aggregated into a weighted composite score whose ranking stability is verified by a sensitivity analysis. To validate the benchmark, we evaluate twelve baselines spanning classical machine learning, temporal deep learning, domain adaptation, transfer learning, and training-mode ablations, complemented by noise tests, physically motivated sensor-degradation tests, leakage-oriented checks, and paired significance tests; the results show that the benchmark produces stable and discriminative rankings across method families. The platform further supports daily submissions, a governed real-time leaderboard with anti-overfitting safeguards, full result traceability, and an LLM-assisted analysis report. By providing a fair, reproducible, and insight-rich evaluation infrastructure, RflyBench-FD aims to support the development and real-world deployment of robust fault diagnosis solutions for autonomous quadcopters.
evidence_items.title: RflyBench-FD: The Benchmark for Quadcopter Fault Diagnosis

The data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25° × 0.25° longitude-latitude grid, providing global ocean coverage. 2.      Data Source The raw data used to develop the CDR of TCWV and SST were derived from observations by three satellite instruments with close local observation time. These instruments are: §   AMSR-E (Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer for Earth Observing System) onboard NASA’s Aqua satellite; §   AMSR2 (Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer-2) onboard JAXA’s Global Change Observation Mission first-Water (GCOM-W1) satellite; §   MWRI (MicroWave Radiometer Imager) onboard the FengYun-3B (FY3B) satellite, developed by the National Satellite Meteorological Center (NSMC) of the China Meteorological Administration. 3.      Variable Description TCWV: CWV represents the total amount of water vapor in a column of air, measured in units of mm (or kg/m²). This variable affects the global water cycle, particularly the frequency and severity of heavy precipitation and drought events, which have significant impacts on human life and economies. SST: SST refers to the temperature of the ocean's surface, measured in units of K. SST is a key indicator of human-induced global warming.

evidence_items.summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Forty-three entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten, a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation, a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight, and a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from.
evidence_items.title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

No quantum advantage, verified patient intention, implanted 4D device, medically validated safety or human stroke-recovery effect is reported.   A LETTER FROM THE THIRTY-THIRD RESEARCH FAMILY A faster algorithm is not necessarily a better rehabilitation system. The first flagship tests the full computation ledger and its matched classical alternative. The second asks whether motor-intent decoding survives hidden cue and gaze artifacts. The third checks real 4D actuator work under material hysteresis. The fourth measures rare latency tails and physical stop-to-zero. The fifth removes every source of assistive power before scoring independent proxy function. The common nonclinical platform contains a matched classical-quantum computation benchmark, anonymized synthetic BCI-like signals, nonliving 4D actuator loads, independent clocks and a device-off held-out task battery. None of these tests establishes empirical quantum utility, clinical motor intention, physical patient safety or improvement after stroke. The companion PDF preserves the 819-page research architecture: 30 dimensionally specified equations, 42 fully recomputable 3D analytic sensitivity grids, 82 chapters of six progressive Mechanism–Measurement–Refutation pages, 200 Research Gates and 33 unbuilt Phoenix prototypes. This notebook opens with nine title-led scientific descriptions and all five official 4D F161–F165 titles for accurate publication discovery. The research workflow couples complete compute budgets, cue-blind signal tests, independent actuation and timing witnesses, functional withdrawal and successor reconstruction. FAMILY 33 OFFICIAL QUANTUM-4D FLAGSHIP TITLES / PUBLICATION DISCOVERY F161 | Quantum Co-Optimization of 4D BCI Rehabilitation Systems at the Limit Core research mechanism: joint constrained optimization of BCI decoding, 4D microtool geometry and safe task budgets. Independent counterworld: apparent quantum improvement is produced by weaker classical tuning, missing input-encoding cost, changed task complexity or unreported infeasible solutions. Proposed blind test: freeze the full objective and hardware accounting; hide feasibility constraints and input instances; replay with classical solvers retuned to the same budget and count every rejected result. Evidential limit: offline anonymous synthetic EEG-like intention and nonliving 4D actuator models, not therapeutic planning or human-device control. F162 | Quantum Motor Intention Decoding and 4D Robot Morphology Control at the Limit Core research mechanism: intent-conditioned decoding separated from cue, gaze, EMG artifact and morphology history. Independent counterworld: the classifier memorizes stimulus timing, recording session, eye movement, presentation order or a controller-generated artifact instead of motor intention. Proposed blind test: blindly shuffle cues and session identifiers, withhold complete sessions, introduce no-intent catch trials, and score false action commands at a disconnected dummy load. Evidential limit: synthetic or properly authorized anonymized offline data and isolated nonliving morphology actuators, never live patient intention decoding. F163 | Quantum-Assisted Adaptive Control of 4D Rehabilitation Robots at the Limit Core research mechanism: constraint-preserving adaptive control of a hysteretic 4D mechanical proxy. Independent counterworld: apparent adaptive success comes from a model that assumes away hysteresis, outside energy supply, simplified load changes or a controller consuming more computation than the action deadline permits. Proposed blind test: blind changes in hysteresis loop, actuator load and sample timing, then inject a stale proposal while an independent relay and force sensor measure actual mechanical work. Evidential limit: sealed nonliving viscoelastic/shape-memory benchtop actuator and synthetic controller requests, not human connected therapy. F164 | End-to-End Latency of Quantum 4D BCI Rehabilitation Systems at the Limit Core research mechanism: deadline-aware full-path latency, heavy tails and independent stop-to-zero time. Independent counterworld: latency appears short because reports exclude queue and encoding intervals, average away deadline tails, share the measurement clock or treat a logical stop as zero physical output. Proposed blind test: blind burst loads, clock skew, network pauses and delayed readout; require an independent wall-clock, shunt and mechanical dummy load to capture physical outputs and deadline misses. Evidential limit: offline time-stamped synthetic EEG streams with hardware-in-loop dummy load; no patient-connected near-term quantum control. F165 | Validation of Independent Functional Gains in Quantum 4D BCI Rehabilitation at the Limit Core research mechanism: device-off function, causal controls and rejection of assistance masquerading as recovery. Independent counterworld: observed apparent gains arise from repeated practice, cueing, spontaneous variation, external work, test familiarity or unrecorded dropout rather than any independently retained capability. Proposed blind test: disconnect and physically remove all power and actuation, test unfamiliar nonliving agent tasks, randomize practice sequence and record every failed or missing follow-up in the original denominator. Evidential limit: robotic and software agent rehabilitation analogues only; evaluating actual post-stroke recovery would require clinical ethics, controlled human evidence and separate authorization. I. NINE TITLE-LED SCIENTIFIC DESCRIPTIONS AND FIVE FURTHER PRELUDES 01 | F161–F165: Five Official Quantum Computing and 4D BCI Rehabilitation Research Titles These five formally registered blueprint flagships are quantum co-optimization, motor intention decoding and morphology, adaptive 4D actuation, end-to-end latency, and independent function after device withdrawal. Their full names identify distinct falsifiable studies, not five labels for the same quantum promise. Take joint constrained optimization of bci decoding, 4d microtool geometry and safe task budgets as a specific case. The candidate says a preregistered quantum or hybrid optimizer can be compared with strongly tuned classical alternatives on the same constrained 4D-BCI problem, but only after encoding, shots, reads, retraining and repair costs enter a single end-to-end ledger. The rival explanation says apparent quantum improvement is produced by weaker classical tuning, missing input-encoding cost, changed task complexity or unreported infeasible solutions. A research team should freeze the full objective and hardware accounting; hide feasibility constraints and input instances; replay with classical solvers retuned to the same budget and count every rejected result and report end-to-end wall-clock [s], energy [J], safe feasible fraction [1], task loss [1], compute preparation [s], hardware calls [1]. Only a blinded difference that survives a strong comparison could justify a narrower technical claim. The most important practical inheritance is a separate clock-and-power auditor with an independently tuned classical optimization team. Compare with tuned mixed-integer, sequential-quadratic, Bayesian and evolutionary classical solvers with matched objective, hardware allocation, tuning effort, wall-clock and energy budgets. Preserve sensor batches, artifact transients, calibration, exclusions and all test attempts; refuse if any hard safety constraint fails, comparison budgets differ, data-encoding time is omitted, or a purported quantum gain disappears under a serious classical baseline. Any proposal involving people or implanted robotic devices would require an entirely new ethics, device safety and applicable regulatory review. 02 | Three-Coupling of Quantum Compute, 4D Physical Action and Post-Stroke Evidence Quantum and classical candidates compete on computation, mechanical responses must be verified independently, and any rehabilitation inference must survive the complete removal of external actuation. Sharing one dashboard cannot make these three causal objects interchangeable. Take intent-conditioned decoding separated from cue, gaze, emg artifact and morphology history as a specific case. The candidate says hybrid candidate decoders must be tested under cue-scrambled and cross-session data so that a morphology action cannot be attributed to intention unless an independent reference disagrees with leakage alternatives. The rival explanation says the classifier memorizes stimulus timing, recording session, eye movement, presentation order or a controller-generated artifact instead of motor intention. A research team should blindly shuffle cues and session identifiers, withhold complete sessions, introduce no-intent catch trials, and score false action commands at a disconnected dummy load and report balanced accuracy [1], no-intent false-command rate [1], decision latency [ms], morphology error [mm], calibration error [1]. Only a blinded difference that survives a strong comparison could justify a narrower technical claim. The most important practical inheritance is an independent cue-blind annotation chain, eye/EMG decoy controller and physical false-action counter. Compare with regularized logistic regression, Riemannian signal features and calibrated temporal neural decoders with identical labeled splits and computational budgets. Preserve sensor batches, artifact transients, calibration, exclusions and all test attempts; refuse if an unverified intent triggers action, cue-only performance matches the candidate, false commands exceed a registered limit, or uncertainty is not calibrated. Any proposal involving people or implanted robotic devices would require an entirely new ethics, device safety and applicable regulatory review. 03 | Central Question and Nonclinical Boundary of Quantum 4D BCI Integration Can a reproducible and safety-feasible gain survive full encoding, readout, optimization, actuation, attention and dropout accounting? Offline signals and a nonliving actuator cannot establish clinical intention recognition, medical-device safety or post-stroke functional recovery. Take constraint-preserving adaptive control of a hysteretic 4d mechanical proxy as a specific case. The candidate says candidate quantum-assisted schedule optimization can propose actions only through an independent constraint shield; its mechanical tracking benefit must survive drift, shape-memory hysteresis and classical model predictive control comparisons. The rival explanation says apparent adaptive success comes from a model that assumes away hysteresis, outside energy supply, simplified load changes or a controller consuming more computation than the action deadline permits. A research team should blind changes in hysteresis loop, actuator load and sample timing, then inject a stale proposal while an independent relay and force sensor measure actual mechanical work and report tracking error [mm], delivered actuator work [J], hard constraint breaches [1], model update time [ms], recovery time [ms]. Only a blinded difference that survives a strong comparison could justify a narrower technical claim. The most important practical inheritance is an isolated load-cell, mechanical work ledger and normally-off physical relay. Compare with robust tube model predictive control, adaptive gain scheduling and classical stochastic optimization with equal predictive model, sensing access and total energy. Preserve sensor batches, artifact transients, calibration, exclusions and all test attempts; refuse if model mismatch leads to unbounded output, computation misses the physical deadline, actuator energy accounting fails, or the independent stop path cannot isolate power. Any proposal involving people or implanted robotic devices would require an entirely new ethics, device safety and applicable regulatory review.

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a central post-training approach for reasoning and agentic large language models (LLMs), particularly when task outcomes can be verified automatically. Comparisons across this literature remain difficult because a reported gain may combine changes to the learning signal, policy constraint, response granularity, data reuse, rollout system, and inference budget. This survey develops a mechanism-driven framework for separating these effects. It organizes methods along three axes — learning-signal type, policy/data regime, and optimization granularity — and decomposes their training stacks into reusable motifs spanning advantage construction, drift control, dense feedback, off-policy reuse, and rollout–update dataflow. We use this framework to synthesize representative method families, analyze cross-motif interactions, and conduct source-bounded case studies of how multi-component recipes and asynchronous pipelines should be interpreted. We further distinguish literature-established diagnostics from survey-defined reporting primitives and provide a matched-budget reporting checklist. Finally, we discuss how these interfaces may transfer to vision-language-action (VLA) models, World Action Models (WAMs), and embodied-agent post-training for unmanned systems, where reports should describe action representation, world-model error, interaction cost, and safety constraints. The corpus emphasizes mechanism clarity and records the maturity of evidence from recent preprints and system reports.

evidence_items.summary: This record contains the trained weights and the data behind the numbers and figures of the paper "Generating grain boundary structures at a specified energy with a symmetry-constrained diffusion model" by K. Miyamoto, I. Okuda, I. Takahara and T. Mizoguchi (submitted to APL Machine Learning). The paper studies the Al Σ5(210)[001] symmetric tilt grain boundary. The code (the symmetry-constrained extension of MatterGen, the evaluation scripts and the plotting scripts) is available at https://github.com/nmdl-mizo/mattergen-interface. Contents: - Weights: the fine-tuned symmetry-constrained MatterGen (proposed epoch159.ckpt) and the unconstrained MatterGen baseline (baseline epoch129.ckpt), with their resolved training configurations and the complete model configuration of the baseline for generation. - Training data: 6,510 relaxed Al Σ5(210)[001] symmetric tilt grain-boundary structures with their grain-boundary energies (training.tar.gz). - Generated and relaxed structures of the main experiment, the additional guidance strengths and the verification runs (generation.tar.gz, relaxation.tar.gz). - Evaluation results: novelty, grain-boundary equivalence, structure filter and the other analyses of the paper (evaluation.tar.gz). - DFT checks: VASP inputs and selected outputs (dft.tar.gz). POTCAR files are not redistributed because of the VASP license; POTCAR SPEC.txt lists the TITEL lines of the potentials that were used. - BCC Fe check: a model for the Fe Σ5(310)[001] symmetric tilt grain boundary (fe proposed epoch189.ckpt), its training data, and 700 generated and relaxed structures (fe .tar.gz). README.md describes the layout, how to extract the archives, and the placeholders used for paths. MANIFEST.tsv lists every file of the extracted tree with its size and SHA-256, and SHA256SUMS gives the SHA-256 of the uploaded files.

evidence_items.summary: For historical network analysis, post-correcting the results of information extraction models is not a matter of perfectionist indulgence, but rather an absolute necessity to ensure the precision required for valid analysis. Standard metrics such as F1 and recall weigh every error equally, which does not reflect the post-correction cost imposed on the historian. This paper introduces an operational procedure for measuring post-correction labour, with the edit action as a unit. Every event is classified into one of eight types, positioned on three axes (detectability, locality and search scope) which determine whether it can be repaired by a deterministic script or a manual keystroke (mechanical) or requires reading or prosopographical research (cognitive). We calibrate the two cost tiers against \SI{78} hours of logged annotation work on our own corpus: 561 manually corrected 19th-century French letters from the circle of the Belgian painter François-Joseph Navez (1787-1869). Finally, the taxonomy is applied to seven NER systems, reordering them relative to their F1 ranking. Our contributions are fourfold: an assessment of the manual post-correction of the HTR output; an operational and reproducible measure of post-correction effort; a comparative evaluation of one closed-source LLM (Claude Opus 4.8), two open-weight LLMs (Qwen3-VL 30B-A3B, Qwen3-235B-A22B) and two French encoders (CamemBERTaV2, d'AlemBERT) under that measure; and a reusable expert-annotated corpus of 561 letters with NER labels.
evidence_items.title: Agréez, Monsieur, mes entités les plus distinguées: Measuring Human Labour for NER Post-Correction

evidence_items.summary: Time series forecasting is present across several domains, such as finance, healthcare, energy, and operations, and foundation models promise to replace the traditional one-model-per-series workflow with a single zero-shot pretrained forecaster applied to these domains. Whether they deliver, and where they stop working, remains unknown. Following a survey (conducted on 1 June 2026 from Scopus) reported in line with the PRISMA guidelines, this study surveys 45 articles across five survey questions, covering what time series foundation models are and how they are designed and trained, how well they perform, what is known about their theoretical learnability limits, what phase diagrams and scaling laws reveal about them, and how controlled synthetic temporal environments are constructed and used to evaluate these models. A taxonomy of how models are built and how they are evaluated shows that the literature concentrates on building and benchmarking time series foundation models. Causal analysis of  time series foundation models' abilities and limitations remains underexplored. We conclude that there is significant opportunity for future research in broadening the evaluation methods applied to time series foundation models.
evidence_items.title: A Survey on Current Practices for Time Series Foundation Model Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus L. Moench) mucilage is a natural, water-soluble polysaccharide obtained from okra pods and is gaining attention as a sustainable moisturizing excipient for topical hydrogel formulations. This review examines the extraction, characterization, formulation, and evaluation of okra mucilage as a natural moisturizing agent. Okra mucilage is primarily composed of pectic polysaccharides, including rhamnogalacturonan-I and arabinogalactan-type fractions, containing galactose, galacturonic acid, rhamnose, and associated proteins. Its abundant hydroxyl and carboxyl groups enable strong hydrogen bonding with water, supporting humectant activity, film formation, bioadhesion, and reduction of transepidermal water loss. Mucilage is commonly extracted by soaking or heating sliced okra pods in water, followed by filtration and precipitation with ethanol or acetone. Extraction yield and functional quality depend on temperature, extraction time, water-to-material ratio, pH, ethanol concentration, drying method, cultivar, and pod maturity. Optimized aqueous extraction has reported yields of approximately 11.87–13.68%, while conventional and microwave-assisted methods can produce mucilage with useful viscosity, swelling, antioxidant, and film-forming properties. In hydrogel systems, okra mucilage may act as the primary gelling polymer or as a co-polymer with xanthan gum, carrageenan, guar gum, carbomer, gelatin, or polyvinyl alcohol. Reported okra-containing hydrogels show high water-holding capacity, shear-thinning rheology, pH-dependent swelling, and improved adhesive strength. A 0.2% okra mucilage-containing hydrogel pad demonstrated superior moisture retention, while an okra-extract emulsion-gel increased human skin hydration for up to 90 minutes without irritation.
evidence_items.title: Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus) Mucilage as a Natural Moisturizing Agent in Topical Hydrogel Formulations: A Review of Extraction, Formulation, and Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Curated datasets of real-world software bugs support empirical research in software testing, debugging, and automated program repair. However, exploring heterogeneous bug collections, comparing fault characteristics across projects, and constructing research-specific subsets often require manual inspection and custom scripts. We present TSBugs Explorer, an interactive visual analytics platform built upon our previously-published dataset of 633 bugs from 16 open-source TypeScript repositories, classified into 11 fault categories. The platform integrates bug records, repository characteristics, dependency information, and taxonomy guidance through coordinated visualizations, interactive filtering, and detailed bug inspection. It supports alternative aggregation and normalization of fault distributions, pairwise repository comparisons, and analysis of differences in observed fault profiles. An integrated benchmark builder allows researchers to select bug subsets using multiple criteria, inspect their composition, and export records in CSV or JSON format. We demonstrate the platform through three research workflows: fault characterization, cross-repository comparison, and task-specific benchmark construction. Functional validation by two authors confirmed selection correctness, visualization consistency, export integrity, and reproducibility across the tested workflows. By making the existing corpus easier to explore, compare, and reuse, TSBugs Explorer facilitates systematic, research-specific selection and export of TypeScript bug records.
evidence_items.title: TSBugs Explorer: Exploring and Benchmarking TypeScript Bugs

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly entering translator education, yet it remains unclear whether they build students' own translation competence or merely improve the products students submit. We combined a validation study on public benchmark data with a 16-week quasi-experiment to test a scaffolded human--LLM pedagogy, the Draft--Diagnose--Revise--Reflect (D2R) cycle, for English--Chinese translation. In Study 1, a rubric-guided error-annotation prompt increased the agreement between LLM feedback and expert Multidimensional Quality Metrics judgements on 2,500 WMT segments for all four models tested; with this prompt GPT-4o reached a segment-level Kendall's $\tau$ of 0.30, on a par with the strongest neural metric, and the highest error-detection accuracy. In Study 2, 179 English majors received conventional instruction, unrestricted LLM access or the guardrailed D2R cycle. Unrestricted access maximised LLM-assisted performance but yielded no advantage in unassisted translation over conventional instruction at a delayed test 12 weeks after the course (Hedges' $g$ = $-$0.08) and produced the largest AI-dependency gap. Scaffolded use produced durable gains in unassisted translation ($g$ = 0.70), a 13\% reduction in error rate and higher metacognitive regulation. Process logs indicated that the benefit was transmitted mainly through lower verbatim adoption of LLM output. Pedagogical design, not LLM access per se, determines whether LLMs support or supplant translation learning.
evidence_items.title: Scaffolded large language model feedback builds durable translation competence whereas unrestricted use fosters dependency

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Clinical registries capture adverse events (AEs) in free-text fields that are rarely analyzed. We developed a reproducible large language model (LLM)-assisted workflow using 11,216 free-text entries from 18,069 patients in the German Stroke Registry; 9,146 informative entries were retained after filtering. Embedding-based clustering showed poor separation, whereas an LLM-guided taxonomy identified 89 leaf labels. On the model-assisted 1,000-entry development set used for model and prompt selection, GPT-5.4 reached F1 92.4% (95% confidence interval [CI] 91.4-93.4). On 300 held-out entries, weighted F1 against clinician consensus was 96.5% (94.6-98.1) for frozen GPT-5.4 labels and 90.5% (87.5-93.5) for locally run Qwen 3.5 27B. For AE concepts with a comparable structured field, free text documented 1,345 additional instances (+19.6% over 6,867 structured instances); it also documented 7,546 instances of AE concepts without a structured equivalent, most often pneumonia, urinary tract infection and delirium. Beyond baseline covariates and the structured AE count, integrated complication concepts increased the area under the curve for prediction of good functional outcome by 0.025 (95% CI 0.021-0.028) and for death by 0.018 (0.014-0.021); gains were minimal after including the discharge National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score. On 1,979 public coronary-trial fragments from the Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov (AACT), the software ran end to end, demonstrating its technical applicability to a second clinical text corpus. In conclusion, this workflow enables structured analysis of clinical registry free text and complements structured adverse-event documentation.
evidence_items.title: Decoding Complications: Large Language Model-Based Classification of Free-Text Entries in Clinical Stroke Registries

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Liability for scam losses is shifting towards banks, yet few interpretable tools can anticipate which fraud and scam complaints will end in redress. This study develops SCAM-XD, an explainable framework that predicts whether a complaint to the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) flagged as possible fraud or a scam closes with monetary relief reported by the company. From the CFPB narratives archive, the study builds a benchmark of these complaints, about half of which human coders confirm as fraud or scams. A large language model (LLM) codes each narrative for scam type, payment rail, authorisation, manipulation cues and signals of the bank's response, agreeing closely with human coding on scam type. These features are combined with structured fields, company identity and text representations in a stacking ensemble, explained with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and linked to a cost-sensitive triage layer. Tested on a later period, SCAM-XD improves significantly on strong baselines across seeds, including a reimplemented topic model approach. LLM features yield a compact, interpretable model that nearly matches a high-dimensional text baseline but do not significantly improve the full model. Company identity is the strongest driver of predicted redress, yet firm identity alone predicts far less well, and payment rail and bank response cues act in directions consistent with liability rules. Under assumed costs, thresholds selected on validation data substantially reduce modelled expected cost relative to standard thresholds, whereas model choice matters much less. Redress depends on both the firm and the facts that determine liability.
evidence_items.title: An Explainable Machine Learning Framework with Large Language Model Features for Predicting Monetary Redress in Bank Fraud and Scam Complaints

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) could streamline research ethics and governance review by automating routine quality control checks. This study assessed Claude 3.5 Sonnet, ChatGPT4o, and Microsoft CoPilot in evaluating participant information sheets against Health Research Authority standards. Six clinical trial applications were processed using 32 standardised queries, with accuracy, processing time, error rates, and response quality assessed by two blinded reviewers. Claude showed the highest accuracy, detected more deviations from guidance, and had the fastest processing time (7.17 ± 0.68 min vs. ChatGPT 13.58 ± 2.2 min, CoPilot 23.25 ± 6.21 min). Hallucination rates were lowest in Claude, followed by ChatGPT and CoPilot. Claude also received the highest response quality ratings (77.6% “very good” vs. ChatGPT 56.7%, CoPilot 45.2%). While all three models were capable, Claude consistently outperformed the others, demonstrating the potential of LLM-assisted quality control while emphasizing the need for human oversight.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating large language models for quality control in research ethics review

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background: Differentiating between bipolar disorder (BD) and borderline personality disorder (BPD) is an intriguing clinical challenge that has attracted research attention, as the multiple co-occurring symptoms such as mood instability, impulsivity, and emotional dysregulation have made the boundary between the two disorders unclear. Recent research in computational psychiatry has shown promise in leveraging the power of knowledge graphs and large language models to enable accurate and inter­pretable decision-making. Methods: The study developed a hybrid framework, KG-Psy, that combines large language models with dynamic graphs. The system extracts clinical entities through GPT-5 while employing multi-step reasoning to find hidden connections within a psychiatric knowledge graph that weighs its evidence-based content. The system performs four main operations, which include extracting clinical entities, creating dynamic weighted knowledge graphs, using GPT-5 to trace multi-step cognitive pathways, and evaluating customized treatment options. The researchers used 310 anonymized psychiatric case re­ports to test their method. Results: KG-Psy achieved better discrimination between BD and BPD than other methods. The model achieved a maximum Precision (%) of 91.5, an improvement of 19%, 10.3%, and 7.4% over the KG-only, LLM-only, and Hybrid-other approaches, respectively. The system successfully discovered un­known cognitive pathways, which it used to create accurate pathway maps and provide treatment rec­ommendations supported by numerical evidence. The results of ablation experiments showed that LLM reasoning, combined with the knowledge graph structure, led to high performance.
evidence_items.title: A Knowledge Graph and Large Language Model Framework for Personalized Clinical Decision Support in Bipolar Disorder and Borderline Personality Disorder: The KG- Psy Framework

evidence_items.summary: The requirement classification technique helps with planning, quality assurance, architecture decisions, and risk management. However, traditional metrics regard all misclassifications as equally costly. In this work, we evaluate Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) with Logistic Regression, TF-IDF with LinearSVC, Qwen3.5-4B, and Gemma 4 E2B IT on PROMISE exp in two tasks: binary functional/non-functional classification and 11-class NFR subtype classification. In addition to common metrics, we provide four risk metrics: Risk-Weighted Error (RWE), Criticality Miss Rate (CMR) by triage level, Critical-Alert Precision (CAP), and Critical Subtype Error Rate (CSER). Uncertainty is measured with 2,000 paired class-stratified bootstrap replicates. LinearSVC achieves the highest accuracy both in Task A (0.907) and Task B (0.752), and the lowest Task B RWE (0.235). On gold-labelled NFRs, Qwen3.5-4B shows the best criticality-triage point estimates: CMR=0.073, CAP=0.911, and CSER=0.127. Its paired CMR and CSER differences against Gemma exclude zero, whereas its comparisons with the two classical baselines remain uncertain. Sensitivity analysis reveals that this advantage of Qwen3.5-4B does not persist when the six critical classes are considered equally important. Its differences against Gemma lose support when Gemma's five invalid outputs are removed. When Task A errors are included in triage, Qwen misses 19/55 critical requirements compared with 7/55 for LinearSVC. Thus, risk metrics give the most meaningful results in combination with class-specific, output validity, and pipeline-level analysis.
evidence_items.title: Risk-Aware Evaluation of Large Language Models for Requirements Classification: An Exploratory Study on PROMISE

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Globally, marine pollution generated by oil spills, plastic litter, and industrial waste poses major threats to the environment, the economy, and human health. Field surveys, optical sensing, and manual sampling are examples of traditional monitoring and mitigation techniques that are frequently hampered by inefficiency, poor precision, and restricted coverage, particularly in large-scale or remote circumstances. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) hold revolutionary potential for detecting, managing, and monitoring maritime pollution. AI-based methods such as computer vision, deep learning, and machine learning have been effectively combined with drone imagery, remote sensing, and in situ monitoring to detect, classify, and measure plastic contaminants and oil spills with remarkable precision. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), transformer-based models, fuzzy systems, and neural networks have all improved pollutant detection, hotspot mapping, and predictive modeling while addressing challenges including noisy datasets and diverse environmental conditions. Furthermore, scalable solutions for real-time maritime waste detection and disposal are emerging from AI-driven autonomous systems that incorporate robotic mechanisms and Internet of Things (IoT) sensors. This study fully examines the current state of AI applications for marine pollutant identification, highlighting methodological advancements and detailing future potential for integrating AI into sustainable ocean monitoring and pollution management strategies.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence for marine pollution monitoring and control

organizations: The Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation
evidence_items.summary: The article describes a set of methods and algorithms that form the basis of artificial intelligence technologies and examines their characteristics and technical features of functioning in relation to solving tasks in criminalistics and forensic expertology. Based on the distinction between artificial intelligence technologies for “general” use and highly specialized technologies, the limits of their application in practical activities are defined.Using examples of “general” use technologies (ChatGPT, Alice AI, Grok, and Qwen Chat), their low effectiveness is demonstrated in terms of studying document details to identify the writing materials by the provided digital image of a handwritten text fragment as well as by the verbal description of a specific writing material as a combination of specific features.Based on the results of a comprehensive analysis of the experimentally obtained data, it is concluded that the technological capabilities of these tools in forensic examination are highly limited when solving tasks aimed at determining the reference group of writing materials. At the same time attention is drawn to the importance of using modern, highly specialized technologies developed for a specific expert task provided that the relevant software will not be the sole means of examination and will be used exclusively by the experts competent in their field and the results of such programs are evaluated based on the expert’s specialized knowledge.
evidence_items.title: On the Effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in Forensic Examinations

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being applied across urological oncology, yet few recent reviews have integrated its use across the major genitourinary malignancies in diagnosis, prognostication, and treatment planning. This scoping review mapped the contemporary literature on AI applications in prostate cancer, bladder cancer, and renal cell carcinoma using a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR)-informed approach. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to 15 May 2026, and 35 studies were included. Across the included studies, AI showed strong performance in selected settings, including an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.91 for clinically significant prostate cancer detection on MRI in the prostate imaging: cancer AI (PI-CAI) study, pooled accuracy of 92.3% for renal cell carcinoma histopathologic classification in pathology-focused meta-analytic data, and high reported AUCs in selected bladder cancer recurrence and cytology-related models. In general, multimodal approaches often performed well and in several studies outperformed single-modality models. However, most studies were retrospective, reporting standards were inconsistent, and prospective validation remained limited. In the wider literature, prostate cancer has received the most attention, with fewer robust studies in bladder and kidney cancers. Overall, AI holds considerable promise for improving precision oncology in urology, but broader clinical implementation will require standardized datasets, external and prospective validation, interpretable model design, and appropriate regulatory and ethical oversight.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in urological oncology: a scoping review of clinical applications

evidence_items.summary: Purpose This paper aims to examine the application of artificial intelligence (AI) to environmental sustainability, with particular attention to ethical and governance factors that shape whether AI contributes to meaningful sustainability outcomes. Design/methodology/approach This paper conducts a structured qualitative literature review of peer-reviewed studies on the applications of AI to environmental sustainability, with particular attention to ethical and governance concerns and emerging research directions. Findings The analysis shows that AI is most frequently applied in climate modelling and forecasting, energy optimization, waste management, biodiversity conservation and water-resource management. Across these domains, AI is used primarily to support analytical functions such as prediction, monitoring, optimization and model-based decision-making. Nevertheless, AI does not automatically generate sustainability benefits. Its contribution is conditioned by factors such as the energy demands of AI systems, infrastructure availability, governance capacity and ethical concerns relating to transparency, fairness and accountability. Practical implications The article provides practical policy recommendations for policymakers and emphasizes the importance of incorporating sustainability criteria into the governance of AI, enhancing the transparency and accountability obligations for climate-related AI solutions, promoting the development of “green AI” solutions that focus on energy efficiency and supporting capacity development and data infrastructure. A short-term, medium-term and long-term research agenda on the measurement and evaluation of AI is proposed for more comprehensive integration. Originality/value This review contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it integrates application-focused and ethics/governance-focused studies on AI and environmental sustainability within a single synthesis.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence for environmental sustainability: opportunities, ethical challenges and future research directions

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) is the dominant surface-code decoder but is suboptimal under depolarizing noise, because it discards the X – Z correlation that Y errors induce and is not degeneracy-aware. We present an exactly anchored diagnostic benchmark for the code-capacity depolarizing channel, not a case for neural decoding. Five decoders (MWPM, correlated matching, belief-matching, belief propagation with ordered-statistics decoding (BP+OSD) and a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP)) are compared with an exact analytic maximum-likelihood (ML) reference at distance d = 3 , with exact per-syndrome ML decisions on sampled syndromes at d = 5 , and with a matched-marginal independent-noise control. Measuring MWPM’s suboptimality by the relative logical-error-rate (LER) reduction that ML achieves over it, the difference between the depolarizing and control channels is 19–32 percentage points (pp) above an 11%–14% floor at d = 3 , and 33–60 pp above an 8%–10% floor at d = 5 . At d = 3 the MLP recovers 90%–95% of the MWPM-to-ML gap, more than belief-matching (82%–89%), BP+OSD (74%–80%) or correlated matching (46%–58%). At d = 5 belief-matching and BP+OSD agree closely yet stay measurably above ML, recovering 79%–91% of the gap, while the MLP’s advantage over MWPM depends on the training budget (crossover near 3.5 × 10 5 samples at p = 0.08 ) and, when adequately trained, recovers at most 17%. In simulated circuit-level memory experiments at d = 3 and 5, the classical decoders keep their advantage over MWPM, the matched-marginal split becomes decomposition-dependent, and the MLP recovers 25% of the gap at d = 3 , T = 2 and, over five training seeds and budgets up to 9 × 10 5 samples, stays an order of magnitude worse than MWPM at d = 5 , T = 5 , with or without validation-based early stopping. Per-shot cost grows 33–97-fold for the BP-based decoders but less than twofold for matching, and batched throughput does not bound latency.
evidence_items.title: Decomposing neural decoders: an exactly-anchored benchmark for quantum error correction

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Human-derived nucleic acids introduced during sample collection or laboratory handling are a longstanding concern in genomics. Sensitive, high-throughput sequencing can capture trace human nucleic acids, potentially exposing genetic information in nominally host-free microbial datasets. We systematically examined bacterial isolate sequencing archives and found frequent human-sequence contamination, with recurrence within projects and marked heterogeneity among libraries, including those sharing sequencing lanes. Human fragments spanned chromosomes and retained population-informative alleles, concordant partial allele states and clinically annotated variants. Computational depletion removed more than 99.99\% of strict human fragments, eliminating measured population-affinity and clinically annotated variant signals while largely preserving bacterial assembly features. Human contamination was also detected in bacterial RNA-seq, with both genome-alignable reads and splice-junction evidence of processed human transcripts. Together, these findings show how incidental human material can become recoverable genetic information in public microbial archives and underscore the need for screening before data deposition.
evidence_items.title: Recurrent human-sequence contamination and recoverable genetic information in bacterial sequencing archives

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Intravitreal injections are the most frequently performed intraocular procedure worldwide. Yet the 50 µL dose is usually delivered with syringes designed neither for volumes this small nor for injection into the eye. Dosing accuracy, particulate contamination and residual volume have previously been examined in separate studies, so trade-offs between these properties within a single syringe remain unclear. We assessed all three properties in the same syringes, including models in clinical use for intravitreal injection that have not been characterised previously. Methods Six syringes were evaluated: Injekt ® F Luer Solo 1 mL, Omnifix-F Luer Lock Solo 1 mL, Henke-Ject eco 1 mL (three-part), Zero Residual 0.2 mL, BD Micro-Fine 1 mL, and Omnican 50 U-100 insulin syringe. Dosing accuracy and precision for a 50 µL target volume was assessed with 23 specialist staff. The dosing data were analysed descriptively, and operator-dependent variability was quantified with a linear mixed model. Residual volume was determined according to DIN EN ISO 7886-1. Particulate contamination was quantified by light obscuration after 7-day incubation of water, with and without flicking of the syringe during filling. Particle counts were analyzed descriptively. Results All syringes tended to overdose, with a median delivered volume of 55.1 µL, and only 45.4% of the measurements were within 45–55 µL. In the mixed model, 22% of the variance of the delivered volume was attributable to between-operator differences, and no syringe type differed significantly in mean delivered volume. Among the syringes measured without a needle, the mean residual volume ranged from 0.18 µL to 23.1 µL; the two syringes with integrated needles showed 0.59 µL and 1.77 µL including the needle dead space. All syringes released particulate matter, and in this exploratory study the particle count was higher after flicking in five of the six syringe types.
evidence_items.title: Performance characterization of syringes used for intravitreal injections: dosing accuracy, particulate contamination, and residual volume

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Deep-learning structure predictors (AlphaFold2, ESMFold) require global context. Modeling outer membrane protein (OMP) loops without transmembrane scaffolds creates an out-of-distribution challenge. Across 28 non-redundant OMP crystal structures (1.40–3.10 Å), isolated loops collapsed, inverting core solvent accessibility (native core RSA: 3.6 ± 0.7% inverted to 58.7 ± 4.5% [AF2] and 62.1 ± 4.8% [ESMFold] for buried positions; mean loop RSA: 32.1 ± 10.0%), yielding 0.00% true negative rate (0/28 retaining core burial; 95% Clopper–Pearson CI: [0.00%, 10.15%]) across RSA thresholds 5%–20%. Intact models preserved burial (AF2: 27/28 [96.43%], residue TNR 96.89% ± 5.6%; ESMFold: 26/28 [92.86%], residue TNR 93.21% ± 4.2%). Mean pLDDT fell from 83.0 ± 5.1 to 66.9 ± 4.8, correlating with backbone Cα RMSD (r = − 0.68, p < 0.001; 4.83 ± 1.92 Å); 27/28 intact proteins (96.4%) maintained pLDDT > 70. Mixed-effects modeling confirmed core RSA increases (β = +28.5%, p < 0.0001). A backbone-centric Cα contact density filter (CDα ≤ 10.17; ≤ 10 neighbors at rc = 8.0 Å) identified exposed loops, achieving pilot residue-level macro-averaged AUC of 0.80 ± 0.08 (pooled AUC = 0.96; n = 3 test proteins). Prioritized Pseudomonas aeruginosa epitopes were assembled into a 93-residue chimera. Explicit-solvent molecular dynamics (4 systems × 5 × 300 ns; 6.0 µs CHARMM36m + 6.0 µs Amber ff14SB = 12.0 µs total; 6.0 µs/force field) preserved epitope exposure (41.8 ± 1.2 vs. 28.3 ± 3.1 nm²; Cohen’s d = 4.8). Predictors require intact scaffolding for OMP loop modeling; CDα provides an exploratory filter for full-length prioritization.
evidence_items.title: Structural Context Collapse in Deep-Learning Predictors: A Benchmark of Outer Membrane Protein Loop Decontextualization and a Backbone-Centric Filter for Surface Epitope Identification
